label: Schedulers Intro
title: Schedulers: The Traffic Controller Nobody Thanks Until It Breaks
desc: Directory index for schedulers/ . Everything in here assumes you already know what a scheduler is in the abstract — this

secs.head: Schedulers: The Traffic Controller Nobody Thanks Until It Breaks
secs.body: Directory index for schedulers/ . Everything in here assumes you already know what a scheduler is in the abstract — this is the "here's the actual landscape, here's how the pieces fit, here's what to read next" primer.

secs.head: What a scheduler actually does
secs.body: Strip away the vendor-specific jargon and every scheduler — whether it's managing a single CPU or a 10,000-node cluster — is solving the same problem: Given limited resources and competing demands for them, decide who runs, where, and when. That's it. Everything else — priority queues, fairshare, backfilling, cgroups, reservations — exists to answer that one question well, fairly, and without anyone having to babysit it manually.

secs.head: Two very different meanings of "scheduler"
secs.body: This word gets overloaded constantly, and it's worth separating the two meanings cleanly before going further — because they operate at completely different timescales and solve completely different problems. OS Process Scheduler HPC/Cluster Job Scheduler --- --- --- Lives inside The Linux kernel (e.g. CFS — Completely Fair Scheduler) A separate daemon layered on top of many machines (Slurm, PBS, LSF...) Decides Which thread runs on which CPU core, right now , for a few milliseconds at a time Which multi-hour/multi-day job runs on which set of nodes, potentially hours or days from now Timescale Microseconds–milliseconds Minutes–days Unit of work A thread or process A job (which itself spawns many processes/threads) Visibility Invisible to the end user — it just happens Extremely visible — users wait in a queue and watch it happen This directory is about the second kind — cluster/workload managers, with Slurm as the primary subject, since that's what the majority of production HPC and AI-training clusters run today. The OS-level scheduler still matters (it's why CPU affinity and NUMA binding are worth caring about — see the parallel execution & affinity guide in the benchmarks series), but it's not what schedulers/ is documenting. ---

secs.head: The job-scheduler landscape
secs.body: Slurm isn't the only option, and it helps to know what else is out there — both to understand why Slurm won the default-choice war on most modern clusters, and because you'll inevitably run into the others on legacy systems, vendor documentation, or job-portability discussions. Scheduler Origin Where you'll still find it Notable trait --- --- --- --- Slurm Open source, SchedMD Most modern academic & national HPC centers, most GPU/AI training clusters Plugin-based, scales to the largest systems on TOP500, the closest thing to a current default PBS / PBS Pro / OpenPBS Originally NASA-developed Many legacy HPC centers, some commercial HPC Mature, well-documented, still common in industry HPC (aerospace, oil & gas) LSF (Load Sharing Facility) IBM Enterprise & pharma/life-sciences HPC Strong commercial support, heavy enterprise integration features SGE / Grid Engine (and descendants like UGE) Sun Microsystems → various forks Older academic clusters, some bioinformatics shops Historically very common before Slurm's rise Kubernetes schedulers (kube-scheduler, Volcano, Kueue) Cloud-native ecosystem Increasingly common for containerized ML training workloads Built for elastic, container-first workloads rather than batch HPC jobs — see isolating GPU workloads for how the two compare HTCondor University of Wisconsin–Madison High-throughput (many small/independent jobs) computing, grid computing Optimized for opportunistic, loosely-coupled workloads rather than tightly-coupled MPI jobs [!TIP] If you're moving between sites or reading someone else's job scripts, the concepts below translate almost directly across all of these — only the command names and config file syntax change ( sbatch ↔ qsub ↔ bsub , squeue ↔ qstat ↔ bjobs , and so on). ---

secs.head: The core concepts every scheduler shares
secs.body: Regardless of which tool sits on top, these ideas show up everywhere — learn them once, and every scheduler's documentation gets easier to read: - Queue / Partition — a logical pool of nodes with shared limits (max walltime, max job size, which users can submit). Slurm calls these partitions ; PBS and others usually call them queues . - Job — a request for resources ( N nodes, M cores, T time) plus something to run once those resources are granted. - Priority & Fairshare — the algorithm deciding whose queued job runs next. Fairshare specifically balances priority against how much of the cluster a user/group has already consumed recently, so heavy recent users don't perpetually crowd out lighter ones. - Backfill scheduling — letting smaller jobs jump ahead in the queue and fill idle gaps, as long as doing so doesn't delay the start time already promised to a larger, higher-priority job waiting for enough nodes to free up. This is why a tiny job sometimes starts before a big one that's been queued longer — it's not favoritism, it's gap-filling. - Reservations — blocking off nodes for a specific purpose (maintenance, a guaranteed-start job, a demo) ahead of time, bypassing normal queue ordering for that block. - Node health checking — automated pre/post-job verification that a node is actually healthy (memory, GPUs, filesystem mounts, network) before the scheduler trusts it with real work. NHC is the common open-source tool for this on Slurm clusters. - Accounting / cgroup containment — tracking and enforcing what a job actually consumes, not just what it requested — this is exactly the gap pam slurm adopt closes for SSH sessions that would otherwise slip outside this accounting entirely. ---

secs.head: Why Slurm, specifically
secs.body: A few reasons Slurm has become the default choice for new HPC and AI-training clusters, in rough order of practical impact: 1. Open source, no licensing cost — a real factor at scale, where commercial per-node licensing adds up fast. 2. Plugin architecture — cgroups, PAM integration, accounting backends (like slurmdbd + MariaDB), health checks, and GPU/topology-aware scheduling are all pluggable rather than bolted on. 3. Proven at the largest scales — it's what a large share of TOP500 systems run, which means the rough edges at extreme scale have mostly already been found and fixed by someone else. 4. First-class GPU/accelerator awareness — --gres , --gpu-bind , and topology-aware placement make it a natural fit for the GPU-dense clusters most new HPC and AI infrastructure is built around today. ---

secs.head: The Slurm architecture, at a glance
secs.body: Every post in this directory assumes familiarity with this shape — worth internalizing once: - slurmctld — the decision-maker. Tracks partition/node state, runs the scheduling algorithm, decides what runs where and when — and enforces account limits, when AccountingStorageEnforce tells it to. - slurmdbd — the memory. Persists accounting data (who ran what, for how long, using how much) plus accounts, limits and QOS definitions to a database, which is what fairshare calculations and usage reporting draw from. - slurmd — the muscle. Runs on every compute node, actually launches job steps, and (with task/cgroup + PrologFlags=contain enabled) enforces resource containment — including adopting SSH sessions via pam slurm adopt . - sacctmgr and friends ( sacct , sreport ) — not daemons, but command-line clients that read and write accounting data through slurmdbd . All of this traffic is authenticated with MUNGE . Every operational task you'll do — a rolling reboot, a security hardening pass, a Slurm version upgrade — ultimately comes down to safely coordinating these roles without letting them get out of sync with each other. [!NOTE] " slurmdbd stores the limits" and " slurmdbd enforces the limits" are different claims, and only the first is true. See Slurm multi-tenancy: who stores the rules, who enforces them. ---

secs.head: Where to go from here
secs.body: - New to Slurm entirely? Start with the official Slurm quickstart for the user-facing side ( sbatch , srun , squeue ) before diving into the admin-focused posts here. - Sharing a cluster between teams? Slurm multi-tenancy covers associations, limits, QOS and fairshare — and the one missing slurm.conf line that makes limits do nothing. - Running more than one GPU generation? Mixing GPU types in Slurm explains heterogeneous jobs, the bare- constraint trap, and why mixed training disappoints. - Already running a cluster and hardening it? Start with slurm-pam-adopt-blog.md — it's a small config change that closes a real, commonly-overlooked gap. - Planning your next maintenance window? slurm-reboot-order-blog.md is the checklist to have open in a second tab while you work. - Wondering how scheduler decisions (rank placement, node allocation) connect to the performance numbers you actually measure? That's where this directory hands off to the benchmarks series — specifically the parallel execution & affinity guide, which picks up exactly where Slurm's node allocation leaves off.

label: The Tale of job.sh and the Snapshot
title: The Tale of job.sh and the Snapshot
desc: When you run sbatch job.sh, Slurm doesn't keep a live link to your file. Instead, at the moment of submission, it reads

secs.head: The Tale of job.sh and the Snapshot
The Tale of job.sh and the Snapshot
Once Upon A Time
secs.body: When you run sbatch job.sh, Slurm doesn't keep a live link to your file. Instead, at the moment of submission, it reads the script, copies its contents into the job record (spooled internally, typically under StateSaveLocation), and hands it a JobID. From that instant on, the job is frozen in time — it carries its own private copy of the script. So here's what's happening in your case: - Job 1 (running) — using the snapshot taken when you submitted it. Editing job.sh now does nothing to it. It's already off living its own life. - Job 2 (pending) — same story. Even though it hasn't started yet, Slurm already took its snapshot at submission time, not at start time. It's sitting in the queue holding onto the old version of the script, waiting for resources — not waiting to "check" the file again.

secs.head: When does your edit matter?
secs.body: Only for the next sbatch job.sh you run. Any submission after your edit will pick up the new snapshot. That's it.

secs.head: Best practice
secs.body: If you want to change what's running or queued: Cancel and resubmit: scancel <jobid then sbatch job.sh — cleanest option. Version your scripts: job v1.sh, job v2.sh, or better, tag by commit hash / date, so squeue output and your script history stay traceable to what actually ran. Never edit-in-place while jobs are pending if you're debugging — you'll convince yourself the fix "should" apply and burn time confused when it doesn't. Slurm treats submission as a commitment, not a promise to check back later.

label: Slurm SSH Access
title: The SSH Backdoor Every Slurm Cluster Has (Until You Close It)
desc: Part of the schedulers/ series. Status: 🚧 living document — this one grows as more Slurm internals get explored.

secs.head: The SSH Backdoor Every Slurm Cluster Has (Until You Close It)
secs.body: Part of the schedulers/ series. Status: 🚧 living document — this one grows as more Slurm internals get explored.

secs.head: The problem nobody notices until it bites
secs.body: Here's a scenario that plays out on unprotected clusters constantly: A user submits a job through sbatch . Slurm dutifully allocates a slice of a compute node, wraps it in a cgroup, and enforces the CPU/memory limits that job asked for. So far, so good — the scheduler is doing its job. Then the same user, out of habit or curiosity, does this: And... it just works. No job context, no cgroup, no resource accounting. That SSH session lands on the node completely outside Slurm's supervision. From there, a user (or a stray leftover process) can: - 🔓 Consume resources that aren't counted under any job's cgroup - 🔓 Escape the job's CPU/memory limits entirely - 🔓 Keep running long after the job that "owned" the node has ended None of this requires malicious intent — it's usually just someone debugging or checking on a running job the easy way. But the effect is the same: your scheduler's accounting is now a polite fiction.

secs.head: Enter pam slurm adopt
secs.body: This is a PAM (Pluggable Authentication Module) module that ships with Slurm, and its job is refreshingly narrow: Every login or process on a compute node must belong to a Slurm job — no exceptions. [!NOTE] Official reference: Slurm documentation — pam slurm adopt

secs.head: How it actually decides who gets in
secs.body: When a user tries to SSH into a compute node, here's the decision Slurm makes on their behalf: The practical upshot: - ✅ Only users with a currently running job on that specific node can log in. - ✅ Whatever they do once they're in — spawn processes, run a quick htop , debug something — stays inside the job's resource allocation. No more phantom, unaccounted-for work. ---

secs.head: Installing it
secs.body: Nothing exotic here — follow Slurm's own installation guide. It typically ships alongside your Slurm build/package, so if you're already building Slurm from source with the standard contribs enabled, you likely already have the module available. ---

secs.head: Configuring it — three places, three changes
secs.body: Per the official documentation, getting this working touches exactly three configuration surfaces. Skip any one of them and the module either won't function or won't have anything to "adopt" into.

secs.head: 1. Slurm side
secs.body: - [ ] Enable the task/cgroup plugin in slurm.conf . This is a hard prerequisite — pam slurm adopt has nothing to adopt sessions into without cgroup containment already active. Walk through the Slurm cgroups guide if you haven't set this up yet. - [ ] Set PrologFlags=contain in slurm.conf . This is the flag that actually creates the "extern" step — the container that SSH-launched processes get folded into. [!WARNING] Jobs launched without PrologFlags=contain don't get an extern step at all — which means pam slurm adopt has no valid target to adopt an SSH session into for those jobs, regardless of how correctly everything else is configured. [!TIP] UsePAM in slurm.conf is a completely different setting and has nothing to do with pam slurm adopt . Don't confuse the two while troubleshooting — chasing UsePAM when the real issue is PrologFlags is a common dead end.

secs.head: 2. SSH side
secs.body: - [ ] In /etc/ssh/sshd config , confirm: This is typically the default already — but confirm it explicitly rather than assuming, especially on hardened or custom-imaged nodes.

secs.head: 3. PAM side
secs.body: - [ ] In your /etc/pam.d config (typically the sshd service file), add: [!NOTE] You can use either required or sufficient as the PAM control flag, depending on how strict you want the enforcement stacked against other account rules already in that file. ---

secs.head: The mental model to keep
secs.body: One module, one PAM stanza, one PrologFlags change — and the gap between "what Slurm thinks is running" and "what's actually running" closes completely. It's a small configuration lift for a problem that otherwise quietly erodes your scheduler's accounting on every single multi-tenant cluster.

label: Rebooting a Slurm Cluster
title: Rebooting a Slurm Cluster Without Losing Your Job (Or Anyone Else's)
desc: Part of the schedulers/ series. Sourced and expanded from a classic r/HPC thread that every cluster admin eventually red

secs.head: Rebooting a Slurm Cluster Without Losing Your Job (Or Anyone Else's)
secs.body: Part of the schedulers/ series. Sourced and expanded from a classic r/HPC thread that every cluster admin eventually rediscovers the hard way.

secs.head: The question every new admin eventually asks
secs.body: "What's the actual order for restarting the nodes? At what point do I drain the compute nodes? Should slurmdbd , slurmd , and slurmctld stay auto-enabled across a reboot? Do I just shutdown -r now a node, or stop the daemons first with scontrol shutdown ? And where does a maintenance reservation fit into all of this?" This is a rite of passage — everyone runs into it the first time they need to patch a Slurm cluster without a) losing queued jobs, b) corrupting the accounting database, or c) getting paged at 2 AM because a node came back up in a weird state and started eating jobs it shouldn't have. Below is the order that actually works, assuming you are not upgrading Slurm itself — just patching/rebooting the underlying OS. ---

secs.head: Before you touch anything: five things to have ready
secs.body: Skipping this section is how a 2-hour maintenance window turns into a 14-hour incident. - [ ] Estimate the work and the time it'll take. Vague estimates turn into angry Slack threads from users mid-maintenance. - [ ] Prepare a small test job. A tiny xhpl instance is perfect — cheap to run, and immediately tells you if compute nodes are actually healthy post-reboot. - [ ] Create a hidden Slurm partition reserved for you (root only). You want somewhere to test job submission before opening the floodgates back to real users. - [ ] Have a node-health-check mechanism ready — NHC (Node Health Check) or equivalent, so bad nodes get flagged automatically instead of silently eating jobs. - [ ] Confirm you have root credentials and OOB/BMC/IPMI console access to every server. Losing thousands of core-hours because a node hung at GRUB and you couldn't remember how to reach its console is a genuinely common, genuinely avoidable failure mode. [!TIP] If you have a test/lab system, dry-run the entire upgrade path there before day D. There is no substitute for having already seen the failure once. ---

secs.head: Phase 0 — Scheduling
secs.body: 1. Estimate when currently running jobs will finish , and schedule your maintenance start time safely after that. Pick your weekday carefully: [!WARNING] Avoid Thursdays and Fridays. Users can't submit new jobs during the blackout, the system sits under-utilized over the weekend, and if something breaks Friday night, nobody's around to help you fix it. 2. Create a reservation with the MAINT flag , starting at your chosen time — with a safe overlap buffer built in, because maintenance windows always run long. 3. Wait for day D, time T. If you have a test/lab system, use the waiting period to dry-run the upgrade path there.

secs.head: Phase 1 — Locking down access
secs.body: 4. Place /etc/nologin on the front-end/login nodes to block non-root users from doing anything unexpected while you work. (Make sure your own root login still works before you do this.) 5. Confirm State=DOWN is set on partitions in slurm.conf — this is your safety net against a badly-restarted slurmd /node grabbing and executing jobs before you're ready.

secs.head: Phase 2 — Control plane first
secs.body: 6. Stop and disable slurmctld , then slurmdbd — controller before database daemon, in that order. 7. Take a consistent backup of the Slurm SQL database. This is your one clean window to do it — everything is quiesced, nothing is writing to it mid-backup. Future-you will be extremely grateful you didn't skip this step. 8. Stop and disable MariaDB/MySQL. 9. Reboot the Slurm and DB servers and perform whatever underlying OS maintenance you actually came here to do. 10. Bring services back up in order: DB → slurmdbd → slurmctld . Check the logs carefully — confirm services started cleanly and that partitions are genuinely showing DOWN (not silently back up and accepting work).

secs.head: Phase 3 — Front-end nodes
secs.body: 11. Reboot the front-end/login servers now that the control plane is confirmed healthy. Re-apply /etc/nologin here too — it gets wiped during the boot process, so it won't persist automatically. 12. Verify InfiniBand, filesystem mounts, and Slurm client connectivity on the front-ends. Kernel version changes are a classic way to break third-party kernel modules (IB drivers especially) — don't assume "it booted" means "it works." Once confirmed healthy, remove /etc/nologin and let users back onto the front-ends. Partitions are still DOWN , so they can queue jobs — nothing will actually execute yet.

secs.head: Phase 4 — Compute nodes
secs.body: 13. Reboot the compute nodes. If they're already empty (which they should be, per your Phase 0 scheduling), there's no real need to fuss with drain state first. 14. Clear the "unexpectedly rebooted" flag by setting node state to idle , and let your node health check mechanism (NHC or equivalent) do its job of flagging anything unhealthy.

secs.head: Phase 5 — Controlled reopening
secs.body: 15. Flip your hidden root-only partition to UP and submit your test job (that small xhpl instance from your prep checklist) there first. 16. If the test job runs clean — open the real partitions. State=UP , and you're done. ---

secs.head: The order, visualized
secs.body: ★ = the one irreversible step in the whole sequence — get your DB backup before touching MariaDB/MySQL, not after. ---

secs.head: Why this order and not another
secs.body: The sequence isn't arbitrary — it follows a simple dependency chain: Bring anything up out of order — say, compute nodes before the controller is confirmed healthy — and you risk exactly the failure mode this whole checklist exists to prevent: a node rejoining the pool in a bad state and silently swallowing jobs before you've verified anything. ---

secs.head: The honest caveat
secs.body: This exact sequence scales down cleanly to a handful of nodes and a weekend maintenance window. On genuinely large systems, expect the process to stretch, and expect pressure from whoever's paying the bills — every hour of downtime on a large cluster can cost thousands of euros , and that pressure is real regardless of how careful you're being. Two things help more than anything else at that scale: a longer prep list than you think you need, and enough colleagues in the loop that the to-do list isn't resting on one person's memory at 3 AM.

label: Slurm accounting & multi-tenancy
title: Slurm Multi-Tenancy: Who Stores the Rules, Who Enforces Them
desc: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro sketched Slurm's three daemons. This page zooms in on the part that makes a

secs.head: Slurm Multi-Tenancy: Who Stores the Rules, Who Enforces Them
secs.body: Part of the schedulers directory. The intro sketched Slurm's three daemons. This page zooms in on the part that makes a shared cluster fair: accounts, limits and usage history. By the end you'll know which daemon stores the rules, which one enforces them, what sacctmgr actually is, and the one missing line in slurm.conf that makes every limit you set do nothing.

secs.head: The limit that wasn't
secs.body: A university buys a GPU cluster. Three labs share it. The vision lab is promised at most 16 GPUs at a time. The admin opens a terminal and runs: sacctmgr says the change was made. The admin closes the ticket. Two weeks later, the NLP lab's PI sends an angry email with a screenshot: the vision lab is running on 40 GPUs. The limit is right there in the database. sacctmgr show assoc displays it proudly. And Slurm is ignoring it completely. Nothing is broken. Slurm's resource-limits docs say that to enforce scheduling policy you set AccountingStorageEnforce in slurm.conf , and its limits option is the one that enforces association limits. Leave it unset, the default, and the limits sit in the database doing nothing. The admin stored the rule. Nobody told the enforcer to read it. That gap, between where rules are stored and where they're enforced , is the whole story of this page. ---

secs.head: Four programs, four jobs
secs.body: Program Kind Runs on Its job --------- ------ --------- --------- slurmctld Daemon (the controller) Head node, plus an optional backup Holds the live state of nodes, partitions and jobs; makes every scheduling decision; enforces limits when enforcement is turned on slurmd Daemon (the node agent) Every compute node Launches job steps, contains them with cgroups, reports back slurmdbd Daemon (the database front end) A database host, often the head node or a dedicated server Stores accounts, users, limits, QOS definitions and job history in MySQL/MariaDB; serves them to controllers and commands sacctmgr Command-line client Anywhere with Slurm clients installed Edits the accounting database through slurmdbd Plus the quiet fifth member: MUNGE , the authentication service. Slurm's resource-limits docs note that slurmdbd authenticates its traffic through a Slurm authentication plugin such as MUNGE, so a controller or command can't just claim to be someone else. A useful way to picture it: slurmdbd is the filing cabinet , slurmctld is the bouncer at the door , and sacctmgr is the pen you write rules with. Writing a rule into the cabinet doesn't make the bouncer check it. How the rules travel, per SchedMD's own architecture slides: slurmdbd sits between users and the database so nobody needs direct database access, and it pushes updates out to slurmctld on each cluster. The controller keeps its own working copy, which is why scheduling doesn't stop for a database round trip on every job. ---

secs.head: Correcting a common summary
secs.body: You'll often see multi-tenancy summarized like this: "accounting, resource limits and historical data are managed entirely by slurmdbd, while sacctmgr is merely a client." Half right: Claim Verdict ------- --------- " sacctmgr is a command-line client of slurmdbd ." Correct. It reads and writes accounting data through the daemon. " slurmdbd stores accounts, limits and history." Correct. It's the system of record, backed by a database. "Limits are managed entirely by slurmdbd ." Wrong where it matters. slurmdbd stores them; slurmctld enforces them, and only if AccountingStorageEnforce says so. "Without slurmdbd , no accounting." Mostly true for multi-tenant setups: Slurm's docs strongly recommend slurmdbd as the front end to the database for security and performance. The precise version: slurmdbd remembers, slurmctld decides. ---

secs.head: Associations: the unit of fairness
secs.body: Every rule hangs off an association . The resource-limits docs define it as a 4-tuple: cluster, account, user and (optionally) partition . Accounting and scheduling policy are both configured per association. Accounts nest, which is how organizations map onto the cluster: A user can belong to several accounts and choose one per job with --account . Each (cluster, account, user) combination is a separate association with its own limits and its own usage history. A typical setup, using sacctmgr : These are standard sacctmgr operations from SchedMD's documentation; they weren't run on a live cluster for this page. ---

secs.head: Limits: Grp versus Max
secs.body: Slurm tracks resources as TRES (trackable resources): CPUs, memory, nodes, GPUs as gres/gpu , and more. Limits come in two families, and mixing them up is the most common policy bug: Family Meaning Example Use it for -------- --------- --------- ------------ Grp A ceiling on the whole association and everything under it , added up across all its running jobs GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16 on vision : the lab's jobs together can't hold more than 16 GPUs Lab or team quotas Max A ceiling on each single job (or each user, depending on the limit) MaxTRESPerJob=gres/gpu=8 : no single job above 8 GPUs Stopping one job from swallowing the cluster Grp limits are budgets for a group. Max limits are size caps for individuals. A lab quota written as a Max limit lets the lab run as many 16-GPU jobs as it likes. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ The vision account has GrpTRES=gres/gpu=16 . Alice submits two 8-GPU jobs; both run. Bob submits a 4-GPU job. AccountingStorageEnforce=limits is set. What happens to Bob's job? It pends . The account's running jobs already hold 16 GPUs, its group ceiling. Bob's job waits until one of Alice's finishes, even if half the cluster is idle. That's the point of a group limit, and also its cost: quotas can leave GPUs idle. That trade-off is why many sites pair hard limits with fairshare, below. ---

secs.head: QOS and fairshare: the other two dials
secs.body: Limits say how much . Two more mechanisms say who goes first . QOS (Quality of Service) is a named policy a job runs under: priority boost, preemption rules, its own limits. A site might have normal , high for deadline work, and scavenger for preemptible jobs that soak up idle GPUs. With qos in AccountingStorageEnforce , every job must use a valid QOS, given explicitly or by default. Fairshare adjusts priority by recent usage. An association that has consumed more than its share recently drops in priority; one that's been quiet rises. It's how a cluster stays fair without hard caps: heavy users aren't blocked, they just wait behind lighter ones. It needs usage history, which is exactly what the accounting database keeps. Dial Answers Blocks jobs? ------ --------- -------------- Grp/Max limits "How much may you hold?" Yes, hard QOS "Under which policy does this job run?" Can, through its own limits Fairshare "Who goes next?" No, it reorders The opinionated default for a shared GPU cluster: fairshare for everyday fairness, Grp limits only for promises you've actually made (like "the vision lab gets 16 GPUs"), and a preemptible QOS so idle GPUs don't stay idle. ---

secs.head: Turning it on safely
secs.body: AccountingStorageEnforce takes a comma-separated list. From the slurm.conf man page and resource-limits docs: Option Effect -------- -------- associations Jobs only run if the user and account exist in the database limits Enforces association limits; implies associations qos Jobs must use a valid QOS; implies associations safe Only starts jobs that can finish within their limits; implies limits and associations wckeys Requires a valid workload characterization key [!WARNING] Turning on associations blocks every user who isn't in the accounting database. On an existing cluster, load every user and account with sacctmgr first , then enable enforcement. The slurm.conf man page also notes that changing AccountingStorageEnforce needs a slurmctld restart, not just scontrol reconfigure ; check the man page for your version. A safe rollout: 1. Populate. Create accounts and users with sacctmgr . Check with sacctmgr show assoc format=account,user,grptres . 2. Enable associations in a maintenance window. Watch for jobs rejected for invalid accounts; fix the gaps. 3. Add limits (and qos if you use it). Verify a test account actually pends at its limit. 4. Keep the rollback ready: remove the option and restart slurmctld . ---

secs.head: When slurmdbd goes down
secs.body: The filing cabinet being locked shouldn't stop the bouncer. SchedMD's slides on the database daemon say slurmctld caches data if slurmdbd isn't responding , so the cluster keeps scheduling with the limits it already knows, and job records wait until the database comes back. What you lose while it's down: changes . sacctmgr edits can't land, new users can't be added, and reports from sacct or sreport won't show the newest jobs. Treat slurmdbd as important but not critical-path, and monitor it so "a few minutes down" doesn't quietly become "a week of cached records." Takeaway: slurmdbd remembers, slurmctld decides, and sacctmgr is just the pen, so a limit only exists once AccountingStorageEnforce tells the controller to read it. For what happens when tenants ask for different hardware in one job, see mixing GPU types in Slurm.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Accounting and Resource Limits - Slurm: Resource Limits (associations, enforcement options) - Slurm slurm.conf man page, AccountingStorageEnforce - SchedMD, "Slurm Database Daemon" (Slurm User Group 2012 slides)

label: **Mixing GPU Types in Slurm**
title: Mixing GPU Types in Slurm - Overview
desc: A three-part series on a question that sounds simple: can one Slurm job get H100s and A100s at the same time? Short answ

secs.head: Mixing GPU Types in Slurm - Overview
secs.body: A three-part series on a question that sounds simple: can one Slurm job get H100s and A100s at the same time? Short answer: yes, in four different ways. Long answer: the scheduler part works fine; what usually breaks is the job you put on top of it. By the end you'll know which way to use, which to avoid, and how to explain the difference.

secs.head: The myth, the correction, and the real answer
secs.body: There are three stages most people go through with this question. Stage 1, the myth: "Slurm can't give one job two kinds of GPU. A job gets one kind of node." Stage 2, the correction: "Oh, it can. There's a thing called heterogeneous jobs. But it doesn't really work." Stage 3, the real answer: Slurm has supported heterogeneous jobs since version 17.11, and there are three other ways to end up with mixed GPUs besides. The scheduling works as documented. What "doesn't work" is something else: putting one tightly synchronized training run across GPUs of different speeds, and paying the scheduling costs that co-scheduling brings. Those are real, but they're about the workload and the queue , not a broken feature. The difference matters. "Slurm can't" ends the conversation. "Slurm can, here's when it's worth it" is what a senior engineer says. ---

secs.head: The route
secs.body: Page The question it answers --- ------ ------------------------- 1 Four ways to ask for mixed GPUs What exactly can Slurm do, and which innocent-looking option mixes GPUs by accident? 2 Why mixed training disappoints Why does a 16-GPU job with 8 H100s run like 16 A100s, and what does co-scheduling cost in the queue? 3 Where heterogeneous jobs shine Which workloads actually benefit, how should admins set up the cluster, and what's the interview answer? ---

secs.head: Who this is for
secs.body: HPC and AI platform engineers running Slurm on clusters that grew over time: a rack of A100s from two years ago, a row of H100s from last quarter, maybe something newer on order. Also anyone preparing for a scheduler question in an AI-infrastructure interview. ---

Try them on a test partition first. Behavior can differ between Slurm versions; the pages note the version a feature arrived in where it matters.

label: 1. Four ways to mix GPUs
title: Four Ways to Ask Slurm for Mixed GPUs
desc: Part 1 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series. Slurm doesn't have one way to give a job different GPUs. It has four, an

secs.head: Four Ways to Ask Slurm for Mixed GPUs
secs.body: Part 1 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series. Slurm doesn't have one way to give a job different GPUs. It has four, and they behave very differently. By the end of this page you'll know what each one allocates, which one to reach for, and why a single in a constraint has quietly mixed GPU types on more clusters than any heterogeneous job ever has.

secs.head: The job that started fast and ran slow
secs.body: A researcher needs 16 GPUs for a training run. The H100 partition has a two-day queue. The A100 nodes are busy too. So she gets clever and writes: "Either kind is fine," she thinks. The job starts in twenty minutes. She goes for lunch feeling smart. When she comes back, the loss curve is crawling. squeue shows the job is running on two H100 nodes and two A100 nodes. Slurm did exactly what she asked: give me nodes that have H100s or A100s. It never promised they'd all be the same. She didn't submit a "heterogeneous job." She doesn't know the term. She mixed GPU types with one character. That's the first lesson of this series: mixed allocations happen by accident far more often than on purpose. To see why, start with how Slurm tells GPUs apart at all. ---

secs.head: First, how Slurm knows a GPU's type
secs.body: Slurm describes GPUs as GRES (generic resources). An admin can give each GPU a type , either in gres.conf or by letting Slurm detect it through NVML. With autodetection, Slurm matches the type you configure against the GPU's reported name, and any substring works: the GRES docs show a GPU detected as geforce rtx 2060 that can be typed as geforce , rtx or 2060 . Admins can also tag nodes with features , free-form labels like h100 or a100 that jobs match with --constraint . So there are two separate labeling systems: Label Lives on Requested with Answers ------- ---------- ---------------- --------- GRES type Each GPU --gres=gpu:h100:4 , --gpus=h100:8 "Which GPUs inside the node?" Feature Each node --constraint=h100 "Which nodes?" Every way of mixing GPUs uses one or both. Here they are, from the most common to the most deliberate. ---

secs.head: Way 1: typed GRES, one kind per request
secs.body: The everyday request names a type and a count: The GRES docs define the form as name[:type:count] for --gres and [type]:count for the --gpu options. One detail matters a lot here: --gres is per node. It asks for the same thing on every node in the job. That gives one legitimate way to get two types: a node that physically contains both. The GRES docs' own example configures nodes with Gres=gpu:tesla:2,gpu:kepler:2 , two kinds of GPU in one chassis. On nodes like that, a job can ask for some of each. Data-center GPU servers are rarely built that way, so for A100-plus-H100 this is mostly a curiosity. Another rule from the same docs: typed and untyped requests must be consistent within a job. If the allocation asked for --gres=gpu:2 , a step can't then ask for --gres=gpu:tesla:2 , and vice versa. So a single, uniform per-node request can't say "H100s on these nodes, A100s on those." For that you need different nodes to be treated differently, which is where constraints come in. ---

secs.head: Way 2: constraints, and the trap in the bar
secs.body: --constraint filters nodes by feature. The sbatch man page lists several operators, and the difference between two of them is the whole story of the researcher's lost afternoon. Operator Example Means ---------- --------- ------- AND --constraint="intel&gpu" Every node has both features OR --constraint="h100\ a100" Every node has at least one of them. Different nodes can have different ones Matching OR --constraint="[h100\ a100]" All nodes have the same one, but either is fine Multiple counts --constraint="[h100 2&a100 2]" Exactly 2 nodes with h100 and 2 with a100 Read the second and third rows twice. They differ by a pair of square brackets. - Plain OR is an accidental mixer . In a multi-node job it can hand you a blend. That's what happened to the researcher. - Matching OR is what she meant: "give me whichever kind starts first, but don't mix." The man page's own example is [rack1 rack2 rack3 rack4] : all nodes on one rack, any rack. - Multiple counts is a deliberate mixer . You say exactly how many nodes of each feature you want. Combined with an untyped GPU request like --gres=gpu:4 , every node gets 4 GPUs, of whatever kind that node has. A SchedMD engineer, discussing the feature-parsing code, described square-bracket counts as "essentially the same as a heterogeneous job." That's a good way to think of it: a lightweight version, where every node still gets the same per-node request. [!WARNING] Audit your users' constraints. On any cluster with more than one GPU generation, search job scripts for --constraint with a bare and no brackets. Every multi-node job using it can land on mixed hardware, and the user probably doesn't know. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Three requests. For each, could the job end up with both H100 and A100 nodes? 1. --nodes=4 --gres=gpu:4 --constraint="[h100 a100]" 2. --nodes=4 --gres=gpu:h100:4 3. --nodes=4 --gres=gpu:4 --constraint="h100 a100" Answers: (1) no, matching OR keeps all nodes the same; (2) no, every node must have 4 H100s; (3) yes, plain OR allows a mix. If you got all three, you already understand constraints better than most job scripts on most clusters. Now for the feature that was actually built for mixing. ---

secs.head: Way 3: heterogeneous jobs, the real thing
secs.body: A heterogeneous job is a job made of several components , each with its own full set of options. Slurm's docs say each component has "virtually all job options available including partition, account and QOS." You separate components with : on the command line, or with SBATCH hetjob lines in a script: Here's what you get, all from the heterogeneous-jobs documentation: - Separate job IDs, one family. Each component gets its own job id ; they share a het job id equal to the first component's ID. squeue shows them as 123+0 , 123+1 . - Started together. Components are scheduled at the same time or not at all. - The script runs once, on the first node of component 0. - srun launches on component 0 by default. --het-group chooses others. - Per-component environment. Variables get a HET GROUP <n suffix, like SLURM JOB NODELIST HET GROUP 1 . - One MPI world, if you want it. srun prog0 : prog1 puts both components in a single MPI COMM WORLD with non-overlapping ranks. Separate srun calls give separate worlds. The docs add two warnings about that last point, in capitals: running one application across components doesn't work with all MPI implementations or Slurm MPI plugins , and mpirun "would require substantial modification" to support it, with no such work known to SchedMD. Admins can switch cross-component steps off entirely with SchedulerParameters=disable hetjob steps . So heterogeneous jobs really do allocate H100s and A100s to one job, cleanly, with each part sized independently. "Can't" is wrong. But notice the shape of the example: the H100s and A100s run different programs . Keep that in mind; it's the key to part 3. ---

secs.head: Way 4: heterogeneous steps, mixing inside one allocation
secs.body: Since Slurm 20.11 , you can also do the reverse: get one ordinary allocation, then launch a single step with different layouts on different nodes, using the same : syntax with srun . The docs' example takes two exclusive nodes with 10 GPUs and gives one step 4 tasks with 4 GPUs on one node and 1 task with 6 GPUs on the other. Two limits from the docs: the step components must run on unique nodes , and you can't request heterogeneous steps from within a heterogeneous job . Useful when the allocation is uniform but the work isn't, for example one process that wants a whole node's GPUs and several that want one each. ---

secs.head: The four ways side by side
secs.body: Way Syntax Mixes types? On purpose? Best for ----- -------- ------------- ------------- ---------- Typed GRES --gres=gpu:h100:4 Only on nodes that contain both Yes Asking for one specific kind Constraint, plain OR -C "h100\ a100" Yes, possibly Usually not Single-node jobs only Constraint, matching OR -C "[h100\ a100]" No Yes "Either kind, whichever starts first" Constraint, counts -C "[h100 2&a100 2]" Yes, exact node counts Yes Simple splits with the same per-node request Heterogeneous job ... : ... / SBATCH hetjob Yes, fully independent parts Yes Different programs on different hardware Heterogeneous step srun ... : ... in one allocation Layout only (same allocation) Yes Uneven work inside a uniform allocation Takeaway: Slurm can absolutely give one job H100s and A100s, deliberately with heterogeneous jobs or constraint counts, and accidentally with a bare , so learn the brackets and audit for the bar. So it works. Then why does everyone who tries to train across H100s and A100s come back disappointed? That's part 2.

label: 2. Why mixed training disappoints
title: Why Mixed-GPU Training Disappoints
desc: Part 2 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series. Part 1 showed that Slurm can allocate H100s and A100s to one job. This p

secs.head: Why Mixed-GPU Training Disappoints
secs.body: Part 2 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series. Part 1 showed that Slurm can allocate H100s and A100s to one job. This page is about what happens next. By the end you'll be able to explain, with datasheet numbers, why a mixed training run is slower than it looks, and list the scheduling costs heterogeneous jobs carry even when the workload is perfect.

secs.head: Doing it properly this time
secs.body: After the accidental mix in part 1, our researcher reads the docs. She learns about heterogeneous jobs and does it properly: component 0 is two nodes of 4 H100s, component 1 is two nodes of 4 A100s. One srun across both groups, one distributed training run over 16 GPUs. It schedules. It launches. It trains. And it runs at almost exactly the speed it would have on 16 A100s. Her eight H100s, the most expensive hardware in the building, spend most of every training step doing nothing. Nothing is broken. Slurm delivered precisely the allocation she asked for. The problem is the shape of the workload, and it has a name. ---

secs.head: The rowing boat rule
secs.body: Picture a rowing boat with eight rowers. Four are Olympic athletes. Four are enthusiastic amateurs. The boat moves as one: every stroke starts together, and the next stroke can't start until everyone has finished this one. How fast does the boat go? The athletes finish each stroke early, then sit with oars raised, waiting. The boat moves at the amateurs' pace . The athletes add almost nothing. Standard data-parallel training is that boat. Every GPU processes its share of the batch, then all GPUs exchange gradients (an all-reduce , on NVIDIA GPUs usually performed by the NCCL library) before anyone can take the next step. That exchange is a meeting point: nobody leaves until everybody arrives. So the rule is: A synchronous job runs at the speed of its slowest participant. Every faster GPU in the job finishes early and waits at the all-reduce. The waiting doesn't show up as an error. It shows up as a GPU that's "allocated" and "busy" on your dashboards while doing no useful work. ---

secs.head: The numbers: how much the fast GPUs wait
secs.body: Here's how far apart the two generations are, from NVIDIA's datasheets (80 GB SXM versions): A100 H100 H100 ÷ A100 --- --- --- --- Dense BF16 Tensor Core 312 TFLOPS 989 TFLOPS ~3.2× HBM bandwidth 2,039 GB/s 3.35 TB/s ~1.6× NVLink per GPU 600 GB/s 900 GB/s 1.5× Memory 80 GB 80 GB 1× Take the simplest case: each GPU gets the same share of the batch, and the step is limited by math, as large training steps usually are. An H100 finishes its share in about 1/3.2 of the time an A100 takes. Then it waits. $$\text{H100 idle fraction} \approx 1 - \frac{312}{989} \approx 68\%$$ Roughly two-thirds of every H100's time is spent waiting for the A100s. Throughput is set by 16 GPUs moving at A100 pace: you've built a 16-A100 job that happens to cost H100 hours. If the step is limited by memory bandwidth instead, the gap is smaller (about 1.6×) and the H100s wait about 40% of the time. Either way, the fast GPUs pay for the slow ones. [!NOTE] These are ceiling-based ratios from datasheets, not measurements. Real training steps mix math, memory and communication, so the exact waiting share will differ. The direction never does: in a synchronous job, the faster GPUs always wait. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ A team has 8 H100s free and 8 A100s free. Option A: one 16-GPU mixed job. Option B: run on the 8 H100s alone. For a compute-bound training run with perfect scaling, which finishes sooner? Work it out in "A100-equivalents." Option A: 16 GPUs at A100 pace = 16 A100-equivalents. Option B: 8 H100s at about 3.2× each = about 25 A100-equivalents. The 8 H100s alone beat all 16 GPUs together , on these ceiling numbers. Adding the A100s didn't just fail to help; it made the job slower. And it tied up eight A100s that another team could have used for their own job. That's the counterintuitive heart of this page: adding slower GPUs to a synchronous job can reduce its speed. ---

secs.head: The features the A100s switch off
secs.body: Speed isn't the only mismatch. The two generations don't support the same things. FP8. The H100 datasheet lists FP8 Tensor Core performance (1,979 TFLOPS dense). The A100 datasheet has no FP8 row at all; its lowest floating-point Tensor Core formats are BF16 and FP16. Training recipes that use FP8 on Hopper can't use it on Ampere. A single run spanning both has to drop to a format both support, giving up the H100's biggest speed lever. Interconnect inside the node. A100 systems use NVLink at 600 GB/s per GPU, H100 systems 900 GB/s. Collective operations that span both kinds of node run at the pace of the slower links, plus whatever network connects the two groups. Memory size, if the models differ. Both GPUs in the table have 80 GB, so that pairing is fine. Mix an 80 GB H100 with a 40 GB A100 and the smaller memory caps the per-GPU batch for everyone, or crashes the ranks that run out first. Software paths. Kernels, libraries and container images are often built and tuned per architecture. A mixed job needs one software stack that runs correctly, and ideally fast, on both. That's more testing for every upgrade, forever. ---

secs.head: Can you rebalance the work?
secs.body: The obvious fix: give the H100s more of the batch, about 3× as many samples per step, so everyone finishes together. It's possible. It's also your problem to build and maintain: - The data loading has to hand out uneven shares and keep them balanced as speeds drift. - Gradients from uneven shares must be weighted correctly, or the training math changes. - The right ratio depends on the model, sequence length and precision, so it has to be measured, not guessed. - Memory limits still apply: a larger share on the H100s must still fit in 80 GB. Teams that try this usually discover that the engineering time costs more than the A100s were worth to the job. Rebalancing is a research project, not a scheduler setting. ---

secs.head: The queue tax: what co-scheduling costs
secs.body: Even with a perfect workload, heterogeneous jobs pay a price in the queue. Every item below is from Slurm's heterogeneous-jobs documentation. All components start together, or none do. Each component might be able to start at a different time on its own. A heterogeneous job waits until every component can start at once. The more components, and the busier each partition, the longer that wait. Only the backfill scheduler can start them. The docs say the more frequently executed main scheduling logic works first-in, first-out and can't schedule all components together, so heterogeneous jobs are left entirely to the backfill scheduler. Their pending reason isn't even set until a backfill pass has looked at them. Backfill makes simplifying assumptions. It typically needs to be able to place each component on a different node to begin the allocation, even if components could actually share a node. You can starve yourself. With overlapping partitions, an early component can grab nodes that a later component needed. The docs give an example: partition p1 has 10 nodes and p2 uses 5 of the same nodes. Ask for 5 nodes in each, and the scheduler may hand some p2 nodes to the first component, leaving a job that can never start. Limits count every component. Each component counts as a "job" for resource limits. The docs' example: a user limited to 2 running jobs submits a 3-component heterogeneous job, which "will have an adverse effect upon scheduling other jobs." Some features don't come along. From the limitations list: Not available Detail --------------- -------- Job arrays Arrays of heterogeneous jobs aren't supported Licenses on later components License requests only on the first component Gang scheduling Not supported Moving between federated clusters The whole job runs on the submitting cluster Magnetic reservations Won't attract a heterogeneous job unless it names the reservation Cancelling one pending component Only the whole job can be cancelled while pending Requeue, suspend, resume per component Leader only, applies to all None of this means the feature is broken. It means co-scheduling is a hard problem, and Slurm makes you pay for it in queue time and flexibility. ---

secs.head: So is it "not functional"?
secs.body: Here's the honest scorecard: Claim Verdict ------- --------- "Slurm can't allocate H100s and A100s to one job." False. Heterogeneous jobs, constraint counts, and even a stray \ all do it "The heterogeneous-jobs feature doesn't work." False. It schedules and launches as documented, with documented limits "One synchronous training run across H100s and A100s is a bad deal." True, usually. It runs at A100 pace and loses H100-only features "Heterogeneous jobs cost extra queue time and flexibility." True. Co-scheduling, backfill only, no arrays, limits per component So the precise way to say it: Slurm's mixed allocation is functional; tightly coupled training on mixed GPUs usually isn't worth it. The feature works. The rowing boat doesn't. Takeaway: in a synchronous job every GPU waits for the slowest one, so 8 H100s plus 8 A100s train like 16 A100s, often slower than the 8 H100s alone, and co-scheduling adds a queue tax on top. So if mixing H100s and A100s in one training run is usually a bad idea, why did SchedMD build heterogeneous jobs at all? Because the boat was never the point. Part 3 shows the workloads where different hardware for different parts is exactly right.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - Slurm: Heterogeneous Job Support (limitations, scheduling, system administrator information) - NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet - NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU datasheet

label: 3. Where hetjobs shine
title: Where Heterogeneous Jobs Shine
desc: Part 3 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series, the last one. Part 2 showed why one synchronous training run across H100

secs.head: Where Heterogeneous Jobs Shine
secs.body: Part 3 of the Mixing GPU Types in Slurm series, the last one. Part 2 showed why one synchronous training run across H100s and A100s is usually a bad deal. This page is the other half: the jobs where different hardware for different parts is exactly the right design. By the end you'll have the rule that separates the two, a setup guide for admins, and an answer that turns "Slurm can't do that" into a strong interview moment.

secs.head: The restaurant, not the rowing boat
secs.body: A rowing boat needs identical rowers because everyone does the same job at the same moment. A restaurant is different. It has a head chef, line cooks, a dishwasher and waiters. Nobody expects the dishwasher to be as fast at cooking as the head chef. They do different jobs , connected by queues: orders go in, plates come out. If the dishwasher is slower, a stack of plates builds up, but the kitchen keeps cooking. That's what heterogeneous jobs were designed for. Look at the example in Slurm's own documentation: one node with lots of memory running a program called server , and 32 other nodes running a program called client . Different programs, different hardware, each sized for its role. Nobody in that example is rowing in sync. ---

secs.head: The rule: mix across roles, not within a role
secs.body: Part 2's problem was that every GPU did the same job , in lockstep . Take either of those away and mixing makes sense. Mix hardware across roles, not within a role. Question If yes If no ---------- -------- ------- Do the GPU types run different programs or roles? Mixing can fit Same role on different speeds: the rowing boat Are the parts connected by queues or occasional messages, rather than a per-step barrier? Each part runs at its own pace Everyone waits for the slowest Does each part have needs that suit one kind of hardware? Put each part where it fits best No reason to mix Three yeses is a heterogeneous job. Here are the patterns that pass. ---

secs.head: Pattern 1: trainer and rollout workers
secs.body: Reinforcement learning on language models often has two roles: - A trainer that updates the model's weights: big matrix math, compute-heavy, benefits from the fastest GPUs. - Rollout workers that run the current model to generate samples: mostly inference, and as the LLM inference series explains, text generation is limited by memory bandwidth far more than by compute. The roles are connected by a queue of samples going one way and occasional weight updates going the other. They don't meet at every step. That's a natural heterogeneous job: component 0 on H100s for the trainer, component 1 on A100s for the workers. Each runs at its own pace. The A100s do useful work instead of slowing anyone down. Two srun calls, two separate worlds, one allocation that starts and ends together. The trainer can find its workers through the per-component variables such as SLURM JOB NODELIST HET GROUP 1 . ---

secs.head: Pattern 2: server and clients
secs.body: The documentation's own pattern, generalized: one component is a coordinator, a parameter store, a database or an inference endpoint; the other is a fleet of workers that talk to it. The coordinator might want a big-memory node; the workers want GPUs. Or the coordinator wants one H100 node and the workers are happy on older GPUs. Slurm gives each its own size, partition, account and QOS, and guarantees they start together, so workers never come up before the thing they connect to. ---

secs.head: Pattern 3: "either kind, never both"
secs.body: Sometimes the honest need isn't mixing at all. It's flexibility: "I can run on H100s or A100s; give me whichever is free first." That's matching OR from part 1: All four nodes are the same kind, so the rowing boat stays matched. The job just starts sooner. For most researchers who think they want "mixed GPUs," this is the request they actually need. Make sure the job adapts to whichever kind it gets: for example, enable FP8 only when it lands on H100s. ---

secs.head: Pattern 4: uneven layouts in one allocation
secs.body: When the allocation is uniform but the work inside it isn't, a heterogeneous step (Slurm 20.11 and later) lets one srun give different nodes different layouts. The docs' example splits a 10-GPU, 2-node allocation into one node with 4 tasks on 4 GPUs and another with 1 task on 6 GPUs. No co-scheduling of separate jobs, so none of the queue tax from part 2. ---

secs.head: Try it before you scroll
secs.body: ☕ Four requests from users. Heterogeneous job, matching OR, or "please don't"? 1. "I want to fine-tune on 8 H100s plus the 4 idle A100s to go faster." 2. "My evaluation harness runs a judge model next to my training job, and I want them to start together." 3. "I don't care which GPUs, I just want to start today." 4. "My simulation runs on CPU nodes and streams data to a GPU model." Answers: (1) please don't: same role in lockstep, the rowing boat; (2) heterogeneous job: different roles, loosely connected; (3) matching OR; (4) heterogeneous job: CPU and GPU components, connected by a stream. ---

secs.head: For admins: setting up a multi-generation cluster
secs.body: The configuration below uses standard slurm.conf and gres.conf parameters described in Slurm's GRES documentation and man pages. Adapt names to your site and try it on a test partition first.

secs.head: Label GPUs and nodes the same way
secs.body: Give every node both a GRES type (for --gres / --gpus ) and a feature (for --constraint ), using the same short names so users only learn one vocabulary: With AutoDetect=nvml in gres.conf , Slurm reads the GPUs from the driver, and the type in slurm.conf only needs to be a substring of the detected name. Check what a node reports with slurmd -C before choosing names.

secs.head: Decide how partitions map to generations
secs.body: Layout Upside Downside -------- -------- ---------- One partition per generation Simple; plain OR can't mix across partitions by accident Users must pick; idle capacity in one isn't visible from the other One shared GPU partition, features to choose Flexible; matching OR lets jobs take whichever is free A bare \ can mix generations in multi-node jobs If you choose the shared partition, guard it.

secs.head: Guard against the accidental mix
secs.body: Slurm's docs note the job submit plugin runs independently for each component of a heterogeneous job, and it sees every regular job too. That's the place to enforce site policy, for example: flag or reject multi-node GPU jobs whose constraint uses a bare without brackets, with a message pointing users to matching OR.

secs.head: Tune the controls heterogeneous jobs care about
secs.body: Setting What it does, per the docs --------- --------------------------- SchedulerParameters=disable hetjob steps Disables steps that span more than one component cluster-wide (useful if your MPI stack can't handle them) SchedulerParameters=whole hetjob Makes cancel, hold and release on any component apply to the whole job Per-user running-job limits Remember every component counts as a job; a low limit can block multi-component jobs

secs.head: Teach users the three lines
secs.body: Most mixing problems are vocabulary problems. Put this in your user docs: You want Write ---------- ------- A specific kind --gres=gpu:h100:4 Either kind, all the same --constraint="[h100\ a100]" Different hardware for different programs A heterogeneous job ( SBATCH hetjob ) ---

secs.head: The decision table
secs.body: Your situation Use Why ---------------- ----- ----- One training run, same role on every GPU One GPU type Synchronous jobs run at the slowest GPU's pace Flexible about the type, but not mixing Matching OR [h100\ a100] Faster start, matched hardware Different programs that start together and talk loosely Heterogeneous job Each part sized for its role Uniform allocation, uneven work inside Heterogeneous step No co-scheduling cost Need job arrays, gang scheduling or migration between federated clusters Not a heterogeneous job Unsupported for heterogeneous jobs Fixed node split, same per-node request Constraint counts [h100 2&a100 2] Lightweight, but you're mixing: be sure the workload tolerates it ---

secs.head: The interview answer
secs.body: "Can Slurm allocate different GPU types, say H100s and A100s, to one job?" "Yes. Since 17.11 it supports heterogeneous jobs: several components, each with its own resources, partition and QOS, scheduled together. You can also get a fixed split with constraint counts, or mix by accident with a plain OR constraint, which is why I'd use matching OR, the bracketed form, when users just want either type. The real question is whether you should. For one synchronous training run, no: every step waits at the all-reduce for the slowest GPU, so eight H100s plus eight A100s train at A100 pace, and on datasheet numbers the eight H100s alone would be faster. You also lose H100-only features like FP8. Heterogeneous jobs also pay a queue cost: all components must start together, only the backfill scheduler places them, and they don't support job arrays. Where they shine is different roles on different hardware: a trainer on H100s with rollout or inference workers on A100s, or a server with a fleet of clients. The rule I use is: mix hardware across roles, not within a role." Takeaway: heterogeneous jobs are for restaurants, not rowing boats, so give different roles different hardware, give one synchronous role one kind of GPU, and give flexible users matching OR. That's the series. You started with "Slurm can't" and "it doesn't really work." You're leaving with "it works, here's exactly when to use it." Back to the overview.

secs.head: Statistics
secs.body: Many enthusiastic people who love to have a great challenge, jump to the unbounded realm of AI, and get amazed by its titles like machine learning, deep learning, architecture, and other words related to this field. But what they don't know is that, the real challenge if where all of this came from?

secs.head: What is Statistics?
secs.body: The field of statistics is a branch of mathematics that deals with the collection, analysis, interpretation, presentation, and organization of data. It involves the use of mathematical techniques to summarize and describe data, as well as to draw conclusions and make decisions based on data. Statistics is a diverse field that encompasses a wide range of topics, including: Topic Description -- -- Descriptive statistics This area of statistics focuses on summarizing and describing the main features of a dataset, such as measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and variability (range, variance, standard deviation). Inferential statistics This area of statistics uses samples of data to make inferences about populations. It includes statistical methods for hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and regression analysis. Probability This area of statistics deals with the study of chance events and their likelihood of occurrence. It forms the basis for many statistical methods and models. Data visualization This area of statistics involves using graphical techniques to represent data in a meaningful and informative way, such as histograms, bar charts, scatter plots, and box plots. Machine learning This area of statistics involves using algorithms and statistical models to analyze and learn patterns in data, and make predictions or classifications based on those patterns. Time series analysis This area of statistics deals with the analysis of data that is collected over time, and involves methods for forecasting, trend analysis, and anomaly detection. Bayesian statistics This area of statistics uses Bayes' theorem to update probabilities based on new data or information, and is particularly useful in situations where prior knowledge or beliefs can be incorporated into the analysis. Computational statistics This area of statistics involves developing algorithms and computer programs to perform statistical analyses, especially in cases where large datasets are involved. Biostatistics This area of statistics applies statistical methods to medical and health-related data, and is used in clinical trials, epidemiology, and public health research. Environmental statistics This area of statistics applies statistical methods to environmental data, and is used in climate change research, ecology, and conservation biology. Overall, the field of statistics is essential in today's data-driven world, as it provides powerful tools for extracting insights and making informed decisions based on data.

secs.head: Key Aspects of Statistics
secs.body: Statistics provides valuable tools for making data-driven decisions, drawing insights from data, and testing hypotheses in a rigorous and systematic way. It plays a crucial role in research, decision-making, and problem-solving across various domains. Here are the key aspects of statistics: Aspect Description -- -- Data Collection Statistics begins with the collection of data. Data can be in the form of numbers, measurements, observations, or responses to surveys and experiments. Collecting data can involve various methods, such as surveys, experiments, observations, or mining existing datasets. Data Description Once data is collected, statistics helps in summarizing and describing it. This includes calculating measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode), measures of dispersion (variance, standard deviation, range), and creating graphical representations like histograms, bar charts, and scatterplots. Data Analysis Statistical analysis involves using mathematical techniques to make sense of the data. This includes hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and various other statistical tests to draw conclusions and make predictions based on the data. Statistical Inference Statistical inference is the process of drawing conclusions or making predictions about a population based on a sample of data. It involves estimating population parameters and assessing the uncertainty associated with these estimates. Probability Probability theory is a fundamental component of statistics. It deals with uncertainty and randomness and provides a framework for understanding and modeling random events and outcomes. Sampling In many cases, it's not practical or possible to collect data from an entire population. Sampling techniques are used to select a subset of data (a sample) that is representative of the population. Statistical methods are then applied to make inferences about the entire population based on the sample. Experimental Design In experimental research, statistics helps design experiments, control variables, and analyze results to test hypotheses and draw valid conclusions. Statistical Software Modern statistics heavily relies on specialized software and programming languages like R, Python (with libraries like NumPy, Pandas, and SciPy), and statistical packages (e.g., SPSS, SAS) to perform data analysis efficiently. Applications Statistics is used in various fields and applications, including market research, healthcare, finance, quality control, social sciences, and environmental studies, among others. Descriptive vs. Inferential Statistics Descriptive statistics focus on summarizing and describing data, while inferential statistics involve drawing conclusions and making predictions based on data. Ethics and Bias Ethical considerations are essential in statistics, as data collection and analysis can impact individuals and society. Researchers must be aware of bias, privacy concerns, and potential ethical dilemmas.

secs.head: Why to Learn it?
secs.body: In is the real challenge to face!! There are many reasons why learning statistics is important, especially in today's data-driven world. Here are some key points highlighted in the provided context: Reason Highlight -- -- Making informed decisions Statistics helps you analyze data and draw meaningful conclusions, allowing you to make informed decisions based on facts rather than intuition or guesswork. Problem-solving Statistics has the power to solve complex problems in various fields, including business, science, and society. By understanding statistical concepts, you can better understand the variables involved in a problem and develop effective solutions. Communication Statistical literacy enables you to communicate complex ideas and results effectively to both technical and non-technical audiences, making it easier for executives and clients to understand the insights derived from data. Career opportunities Knowledge of statistics is highly valued in the job market, particularly in fields related to data science. Having a strong foundation in statistics can open up new career possibilities and enhance your professional prospects. Versatility Statistics is applicable in a wide range of industries and domains, from finance and economics to medicine and social sciences. Learning statistics can therefore broaden your horizons and enable you to work in diverse fields. Essential toolkit for data science Statistics is a fundamental component of data science, and proficiency in statistical analysis is crucial for working with large datasets, identifying trends, and developing predictive models. Low-risk way to test the waters Online courses and MOOCs offer a low-risk opportunity to explore the field of data science and statistics without committing to a long-term program. Skill up for the future With the increasing demand for data-driven decision-making, learning statistics can future-proof your career and ensure you remain competitive in the ever-evolving job market. Fills talent gaps Companies are looking for professionals skilled in statistics and data science to fill talent gaps. By acquiring these skills, you can contribute to solving this problem and enhancing organizational performance. Enhances data storytelling Statistics helps you present data in a compelling narrative, making it easier for stakeholders to comprehend and act upon the insights gained from data analysis. In summary, learning statistics can benefit you in numerous ways, both personally and professionally. It can improve your ability to make informed decisions, enhance your problem-solving skills, increase your earning potential, and prepare you for a successful career in data science.

secs.head: How to get started?
secs.body: Studying statistics can be a fascinating and rewarding pursuit, as it involves the use of mathematical techniques to analyze and interpret data. Here are some steps you can take to get started: Step Details -- -- Learn the basics Before diving into statistics, it's important to have a solid understanding of basic math concepts such as algebra, geometry, and calculus. Brush up on these subjects if you need to, or take a refresher course to make sure you have a strong foundation. Take an introductory statistics course Look for a course that covers the basics of statistical analysis, including probability, descriptive statistics, inferential statistics, and statistical visualization. Many colleges and universities offer introductory statistics courses, or you can find online courses through websites like Coursera, edX, or Khan Academy. Get familiar with statistical software Statistical software is used to analyze and visualize data, and there are many different programs available. Some popular options include R, Python, Excel, and SPSS. Choose one that interests you and start learning how to use it. Practice with real-world data Once you have a good grasp of statistical concepts and have learned how to use statistical software, practice applying your skills to real-world data. You can find datasets online or collect your own data from experiments, surveys, or other sources. Use statistical methods to analyze the data and draw conclusions. Read books and articles There are many great books and articles on statistics that can help deepen your understanding of the subject. Some classic texts include "Statistics in Plain English" by Timothy C. Urdan and "How to Lie with Statistics" by Darrell Huff. Keep up with new developments in the field by reading academic journals or following stats bloggers. Join a community Connecting with others who share your interest in statistics can be a great way to learn and stay motivated. Look for local meetups, join online forums, or participate in social media groups focused on statistics. Consider further education If you're serious about becoming an expert in statistics, consider pursuing a degree in statistics or a related field. Many colleges and universities offer undergraduate and graduate degrees in statistics, and there are also online certification programs available. Be Patient and Persistent Statistics can be complex, but with patience and persistence, you can master it. Take your time to understand each concept before moving on to more advanced topics. Remember that learning statistics takes time and practice, so don't get discouraged if it doesn't come easily at first. With persistence and dedication, you can become proficient in this fascinating field.

secs.head: Curriculum
secs.body: There are various of books and courses explaining how to study Statistics, but they are all agree on common topics one should study well. The curriculum in studying statistics typically covers a range of topics, including: Topic Description -- -- Introduction to Statistics This course provides an overview of statistical concepts, methods, and applications. Students learn how to summarize and describe data, visualize data using graphs and plots, and understand basic probability concepts. Probability Theory This course delves deeper into probability theory, covering topics such as conditional probability, independence, random variables, and probability distributions (Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, Normal, etc.). Statistical Methods This course introduces students to common statistical methods, including hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and regression analysis. Students learn how to apply these methods to real-world problems and interpret the results. Statistical Analysis This course focuses on practical data analysis skills, teaching students how to use software packages like R or Python to perform statistical computations and create visualizations. Linear Algebra This course provides a foundational understanding of linear algebra, which is essential for advanced statistical modeling and machine learning techniques. Topics covered include vector operations, matrix multiplication, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors. Calculus A course in calculus is often required for statistics majors, as it provides a solid foundation for understanding statistical modeling and inference. Topics covered include limits, derivatives, integrals, and optimization techniques. Experimental Design This course teaches students how to design and conduct experiments, including randomized controlled trials. Students learn how to identify causality, minimize bias, and optimize experimental designs. Survey Sampling This course covers the principles and practices of survey sampling, including questionnaire design, sampling frames, and response rates. Students learn how to design surveys that accurately reflect population characteristics. Time Series Analysis This course introduces students to time series models and their applications in finance, economics, and other fields. Students learn how to model and forecast time series data using ARIMA, SARIMA, and other techniques. Advanced Statistical Modeling This course builds on earlier statistical methods courses, introducing students to more advanced modeling techniques such as generalized linear models (GLMs), mixed effects models, and Bayesian inference. Data Mining This course teaches students how to mine and analyze large datasets, including data preprocessing, feature selection, clustering, and classification techniques. Machine Learning This course introduces students to machine learning algorithms, including supervised and unsupervised learning methods. Students learn how to implement these algorithms using popular libraries like scikit-learn and TensorFlow. Data Visualization This course focuses on creating clear and effective visualizations of data, teaching students how to use tools like Tableau, Power BI, or D3.js to communicate insights to various audiences. Big Data Analytics This course covers the challenges and opportunities associated with big data, including distributed computing, data storage, and scalable analytics techniques. Students learn how to work with large datasets using tools like Hadoop, Spark, and NoSQL databases. Ethics in Statistics This course discusses ethical considerations when working with data, including privacy concerns, data confidentiality, and responsible data sharing practices. These courses provide a well-rounded education in statistics, preparing students for careers in data analysis, research, and academia. Elective courses may also be available in specialized areas like biostatistics, computational statistics, or quantitative finance.
