secs.head: Section: Installing a New Virtual Machine
secs.body: Info Detials - - Motivation In this section, you'll learn how to install a new virtual machine. Whether you're setting up a testing environment, running a different Linux distribution, or creating a dedicated development environment, understanding the process is essential. Objective By the end of this section, you'll be able to create a new virtual machine using the virt-install command, install an operating system of your choice, and manage its basic configuration. Workspace We'll work with the virt-install command to create a new virtual machine. You'll need an ISO image of the operating system you want to install. We'll go through the command's syntax, explore options, and provide code examples. Illustration You'll understand how to use the virt-install command to create a virtual machine and install an operating system. The provided code examples will guide you through the process.

secs.head: Commands: virt-install
secs.body: Command Description Syntax Key Features Switches - - - - - virt-install Command-line tool for creating and installing virtual machines. It provides a convenient way to create, configure, and install virtualized instances of various operating systems. It's commonly used in KVM (Kernel-Based Virtual Machine) environments. virt-install [OPTIONS] - Creating a new virtual machine.</br - Installing an operating system.</br -Customizing virtual machine settings. --name: Specifies the name of the virtual machine.</br --memory: Sets the amount of memory allocated to the virtual machine.</br --vcpus: Specifies the number of virtual CPUs.</br --cdrom: Points to the ISO image for the operating system installation.</br --disk: Defines the virtual disk's storage.</br --network NETWORK: Configures the virtual machine's network.

secs.head: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
secs.body: Q1: What is the primary purpose of creating a virtual machine? - Answer: The primary purpose of creating a virtual machine is to simulate a separate, self-contained computing environment within a physical host. This allows you to run multiple operating systems on a single physical server, making efficient use of hardware resources, facilitating testing and development, and enhancing system management. Q2: Can I install any operating system on a virtual machine using virt-install? - Answer: Yes, you can install a wide range of operating systems using virt-install. As long as you have the ISO image of the desired operating system, you can use virt-install to create a virtual machine and install it. Q3: How can I manage the resources of a virtual machine created with virt-install? - Answer: You can manage the resources of a virtual machine by specifying options such as memory, CPU cores, and disk size when using virt-install. Additionally, you can later modify these settings using tools like virsh to adapt to the virtual machine's requirements. Q4: Is it possible to install multiple virtual machines on the same physical server? - Answer: Yes, you can create and run multiple virtual machines on a single physical server. The number of virtual machines you can run depends on the server's hardware resources, but virtualization platforms like KVM are designed to support multiple virtual machines on a single host. Q5: How can I access the virtual machine after it's created? - Answer: Once a virtual machine is created, you can access it through various methods, including remote desktop access or SSH. The specific method depends on the operating system you installed and its configuration.

title: System Administration - Under the Hood

secs.head: System Administration - Under the Hood
secs.body: The target of this page is to learn more deeper things that come to our minds.

secs.head: 1. SCP - Why it's secured?
secs.body: - The cp in scp comes from the Unix command cp (copy). - But unlike cp, which copies files locally, scp allows copying across networked systems. - The “secure” part comes from the fact that it uses SSH (Secure Shell) to handle both: 1. Authentication (verifying who you are), and 2. Encryption (protecting the data in transit). So, it’s essentially: cp + SSH = scp (a “secure” networked copy) .

secs.head: How it Works Under The Hood?
secs.body: 1. SSH As The Transport Layer : scp doesn't reinvent network security; it delegates it to SSH. When you run: 1. It starts an SSH session to remote . 2. SSH performs Key exchange (usually using RSA, ECDSA, or Ed25519) to establish a shared secret. 3. The session is encrypted (commonly via AES or ChaCha20) and authenticated (via your private key or password) - At this point, you have got a secure channel ; similar to what happens when you log in using ssh . 2. The SCP Protocol : Once the SSH tunnel is established, the actual file transfer happens using a simple, custom protocol . 1. The client sends control messages like c0644 12345 filename\n (meaning "create a file with mode 0644 and size 12345 bytes"). 2. The server replies with acknowledgments ( \0 or error codes). 3. The file data is streamed directly afterward, byte-for-byte. 4. When complete, both sides send a final null byte ( \0 ) to mark success. - So, the SSH connection acts as a secure "pipe" for these structured commands and raw bytes.

secs.head: Direction Matters
secs.body: Running: Your local Machine: 1. Starts an SSH connection to remote . 2. On the remote system, SSH launches a command: scp -t /tmp/ , where -t means "I'm the target"; expects to receive files. Your local scp process then sends the file data to that remote process, So: - local = sender - Remote = receiver Now, flipping it: - Here, your local command wants to fetch a file from the remote. So the logic inverts: 1. Your local scp again open a SSH session. 2. But this time it tells the remote host to run: scp -f /tmp/file.txt , where -f means "I'm the source"; provide files. Now: - Remote = Sender - Local = Receiver

secs.head: Who opens the SSH Connection?
secs.body: YOU!! - The machine where you run the scp command - always initiate the SSH connection. Where you type: - It's said: Hey SSH, connect to user@remote , and once you're in, run a remote scp process for me. - Local: starts SSH → connects to remote. - Remote: does not initiate anything; it just receives that SSH session and executes whatever command the SSH request tells it to.

secs.head: What happens after SSH connects
secs.body: Here’s the subtle part — once SSH is established, the local scp tells the remote SSH daemon to run scp in either send or receive mode depending on direction. Let’s check both cases: 1- Upload (local → remote) 1. Local opens SSH connection to remote. 2. Remote SSH daemon spawns scp -t /tmp/ (-t = “target mode”, i.e. receive mode). 3. Local scp sends file data to that process. So: - Connection initiated by: local - Remote mode: -t (receive) - Local mode: send 2- Download (remote → local) 1. Local opens SSH connection to remote (still you initiating!). 2. Remote SSH daemon spawns scp -f /tmp/file.txt (-f = “from mode”, i.e. send mode). 3. Local scp receives the file from that process. So again: - Connection initiated by: local - Remote mode: -f (send) - Local mode: receive

secs.head: 2. Directory is a Logical Container
secs.body: What a catch phrase! It was from Chapter-3 in HPC book: "High Performance Computing - Modern Systems and Practices".

secs.head: 1. What the Phrase Assumes?
secs.body: 1. A directory isn't physical entity; it does not "contain" files on disk the way a folder contains papers. 2. It's logical, meaning it's a data structure that organize references -- essentially, metadata pointing to where files are actually stored. 3. It's independent of the physical layout on storage device. The same directory structure could map to files distributed across many disks or nodes (as in Lustre, BeeGFS, or GPFS).

secs.head: 2. What's True and what's easy to misunderstand?
secs.body: The definition is accurate in that directories hold references to file inodes (or equivalent structures), not the file data itself. But it’s incomplete if we take “logical” too loosely: - Directories are implemented physically on disk — usually as tables or trees of entries mapping filenames to inode numbers. - So they’re not purely abstract; they’re a logical abstraction backed by a physical data structure. You could reframe it as:

secs.head: 3. Unix Like System ?!
secs.body: A Unix-like system refers to any os that behaves similarly to the original UNIX, follows its design philosophy, and often implements its standards, but isn't necessarily derived directly from the original UNIX source code.

secs.head: 1. Historical Context
secs.body: - UNIX was developed in the late 1960s at Bell Labs by Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie, and others. - Over time, UNIX became both a technical model (its architecture, tools, and philosophy) and a cultural model (its simplicity, modularity, and text-based approach). When newer systems adopted its design ideas — but not its code, they became known as “Unix-like.”

secs.head: 2. Core Traits of Unix-like Systems
secs.body: They generally share these key features: - File system hierarchy : Everything is a file — devices, sockets, text, all accessed through file-like interfaces. - Multiuser, multitasking model : Designed from the start for multiple users and concurrent processes. - Command-line shell : Interaction primarily through text commands (e.g., bash, zsh, tcsh). - Small, composable utilities : Tools that “do one thing well” and can be combined via pipes ( ) and redirection. - POSIX compliance: They follow the Portable Operating System Interface standard, which defines UNIX-like APIs and behavior.

secs.head: Node Health Check - Overview
secs.body: An eleven-part series on LBNL Node Health Check (NHC) , the small bash framework that big HPC clusters trust to decide whether a compute node deserves a job. Read it in order the first time; come back to the troubleshooting page and cheat sheet whenever a node misbehaves at 2 AM.

secs.head: Who this is for
secs.body: Cluster admins and HPC/AI platform engineers who run Slurm (or PBS, or Grid Engine, or even Kubernetes) and are tired of one sick node quietly eating a queue full of jobs. You should be comfortable with a root shell and slurm.conf . Bash wizardry is helpful for part 6, not required before it.

label: 1. Why NHC
title: Why Your Cluster Needs a Bouncer
desc: Part 1 of the Node Health Check series. No commands to run yet. Grab the tea, this one is the "why" and the mental model

secs.head: Why Your Cluster Needs a Bouncer
secs.body: Part 1 of the Node Health Check series. No commands to run yet. Grab the tea, this one is the "why" and the mental model everything else hangs on.

secs.head: The night one node ate 400 jobs
secs.body: Picture cn042 . Its /scratch Lustre mount dropped at 23:10. Everything else on the node is fine: slurmd is up, it answers pings, the scheduler sees it as IDLE . So the scheduler does exactly what it's built to do. It hands cn042 a job. The job dies in two seconds because /scratch/$USER doesn't exist. cn042 is now idle again, and it's the most available node in the partition, so it gets the next job. And the next. By morning, 400 jobs have "completed" in a few seconds each, users are filing tickets about their "broken code", and your job-failure dashboard looks like a heart monitor in a horror film. HPC folks call this a black-hole node : a node that fails fast and therefore looks permanently available, sucking in work like a drain. The faster your scheduler, the bigger the hole. The fix isn't a smarter scheduler. It's a bouncer at the door : something on every node that asks, every few minutes and before work lands, "are you actually fit to run a job?" , and if the answer is no, takes the node out of rotation with a reason a human can read. [!NOTE] Slurm, PBS/TORQUE and friends all have a hook for exactly this, usually called a node health check program . They provide the hook. You provide the program. NHC is the program almost everybody ends up using. ---

secs.head: Meet NHC
secs.body: LBNL Node Health Check (NHC) was started at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in late 2010 (it was called Warewulf NHC until 1.4.2) and has been running in production on clusters of every size since. It's maintained by Michael Jennings at github.com/mej/nhc, BSD-style licensed, and its latest release is 1.5 (October 2026). Why did it win over the thousand home-grown healthcheck.sh scripts out there? Its design goals, straight from the project: Goal What it means in practice ------ --------------------------- Reliable A watchdog timer kills hung checks, and NHC itself, so a dead NFS server can't wedge your node's health check forever. Fast Written almost entirely in native bash (4.3+), avoiding grep / awk / sed forks wherever possible. Less overhead, less OS jitter for your MPI jobs. Flexible Anything you can write as a shell function can be a check. Extensible Drop a .nhc file in the scripts directory, reference the check in the config, done. Reusable One config file for the whole cluster, with per-host targeting. Runs from the RM daemon, cron, or by hand via pdsh / clush . Big users publish their own extensions on top of it. Azure's AzNHC is NHC plus GPU, NVLink, InfiniBand and NCCL checks for their AI VMs, and LANL contributed GPU, Kubernetes and network modules upstream. ---

secs.head: How it works, in one picture
secs.body: A few things worth burning into memory: 1. One config for the whole cluster. Every line in nhc.conf looks like target check . Each node only runs the lines whose target matches its own hostname. More on this in part 3. 2. First failure wins (by default). NHC stops at the first failing check, reports it and exits non-zero. Use -a when you want to see every failure, which is exactly what you want while debugging. 3. Silence is golden. A healthy run prints nothing and exits 0 . Details go to /var/log/nhc.log . 4. NHC takes action itself. The scheduler only runs the program. Slurm's own docs say any action must be performed by the program, and NHC's helper scripts do the draining and resuming. ---

secs.head: The "NHC:" handshake
secs.body: This is the single most important idea in the series, so it gets its own section. When NHC drains a node, it writes a reason that starts with NHC: : When a later run passes, NHC only resumes the node if the current reason still starts with NHC: . If the node is drained with no reason, or with a reason someone else wrote, NHC leaves it alone. That one rule gives you a clean ownership contract: Who drained it Reason looks like Will NHC auto-resume it? ---------------- ------------------- -------------------------- NHC NHC: <failure message ✅ Yes, as soon as checks pass again You, for maintenance HW ticket 4711: DIMM swap ❌ No, it's yours until you resume it Anyone, no reason given (empty) ❌ No, by default [!TIP] Want NHC to keep its hands off a node it drained, say while you investigate? Just change the reason: scontrol update nodename=cn042 reason="ahmed: investigating lustre" . The node stays drained and NHC no longer considers it its own. ---

secs.head: Four moments to check a node
secs.body: Health checks aren't one thing. Mature sites check at several moments, each with a different budget: Moment Trigger Time budget Good for -------- --------- ------------- ---------- Boot / daemon start slurmd startup, before it registers Seconds to a minute "Did this node come up right?" Mounts, NICs, GPUs present, BIOS settings Periodic HealthCheckInterval timer Well under a minute, every few minutes Cheap, continuous checks: mounts, daemons, memory, link state Job boundaries Prolog / Epilog Seconds (it delays jobs!) "Is it safe to start?" / "Did the last job break something?" On demand / deep You, cron, after a drain Minutes are fine Stress tests, DCGM level 2-3 diagnostics, burn-in NHC can serve all four with contexts : separate configs for the same binary (see part 3). The golden rule: the more often a check runs, the cheaper it must be. ---

secs.head: What NHC is not
secs.body: Knowing the edges saves you from asking it to do things it was never built for: - Not a monitoring system. It answers a yes/no question about one node right now. Trends, graphs and capacity planning belong in Prometheus, Grafana and friends. - Not a hardware diagnostic suite. It can call dcgmi diag , memtester or vendor tools, but it doesn't replace them. - Not a cluster-wide performance validator. A single slow GPU or a degraded fabric path can pass every per-node check and still drag down a 512-GPU job. That takes multi-node tests (NCCL, MPI benchmarks). - Not magic. It only finds what you tell it to look for. Your config is your health policy. ---

secs.head: Where we go next
secs.body: Enough theory. In part 2 we get NHC built, installed and passing its own test suite on a node. Takeaway: a fast-failing node looks like the most available node in the cluster. NHC is the bouncer that drains it with a readable NHC: reason, and resumes it once it's healthy again, without touching nodes a human drained.

label: 2. Build and install
title: Build and Install NHC
desc: Part 2 of the Node Health Check series. By the end of this page NHC is installed on a node, its 800-odd unit tests are g

secs.head: Build and Install NHC
secs.body: Part 2 of the Node Health Check series. By the end of this page NHC is installed on a node, its 800-odd unit tests are green, and you know where every file lives.

secs.head: Pick your route
secs.body: Route Use it when Effort ------- ------------- -------- A. Release RPM RHEL-family nodes and you just want the stable release ☕ B. Release tarball Ubuntu/Debian, SUSE without OBS, or a custom prefix ☕☕ C. Git tree You need an unreleased fix, or you plan to contribute ☕☕☕ SUSE folks have a fourth door: packages on the openSUSE Build Service ( network:cluster/warewulf-nhc ). NHC is noarch . It's bash scripts plus a few helpers, so there's nothing to compile. "Building" here means generating the install layout and packaging it. ---

secs.head: Before you start: the one trap everyone falls into
secs.body: Every GitHub release page shows "Source code (zip)" and "Source code (tar.gz)" at the bottom of the assets list. Do not use those. GitHub generates them from the Git tree, and they lack the generated configure script and friends, so ./configure won't exist. Grab the lbnl-nhc-<version .tar.xz asset that the NHC team uploaded instead. [!WARNING] If you see bash: ./configure: No such file or directory , you downloaded the GitHub auto-archive. Either grab the real tarball or treat it as a Git checkout (Route C) and run ./autogen.sh first. Requirements are refreshingly short: bash 4.3 or newer, the usual coreutils, and make . Route C additionally needs autoconf and automake . Upstream commits to supporting the two or three most recent RHEL releases still in vendor support. ---

secs.head: Route A: release RPM (RHEL, Rocky, Alma, Oracle)
secs.body: 1. Open the latest release and copy the link of the RPM matching your EL version. 2. Install it: 3. No RPM for your exact EL version? Rebuild the source RPM: [!NOTE] The old LBNL-hosted Yum repo is gone. For a fleet, mirror the RPM into your own repo (Pulp, Satellite, a plain createrepo directory) instead of pointing hundreds of nodes at GitHub. ---

secs.head: Route B: release tarball (any distro)
secs.body: On Debian/Ubuntu you'll often see --libexecdir=/usr/lib instead, so helpers land in /usr/lib/nhc (Azure's Ubuntu images do this). Either works, as long as you're consistent across the fleet. Want a .deb instead of make install sprinkling files around? Wrap the install with your packaging tool of choice ( checkinstall , fpm , or a proper debian/ directory). Your future self, running dpkg -L during an incident, will thank you. ---

secs.head: Route C: straight from Git
secs.body: Now either install directly, or produce RPMs the way upstream does: [!TIP] NHC deliberately avoids nhc.in -style generated files, so you can run ./nhc directly from a clone. Handy for testing a fix before packaging it. ---

secs.head: Where everything lands
secs.body: Whichever route you took (with the prefixes above), you get this layout: Path What it is ------ ----------- /usr/sbin/nhc The driver script. This is what Slurm will run. /usr/sbin/nhc-genconf Scans a node and writes a starter config (part 3). /usr/sbin/nhc-wrapper Runs NHC from cron/loops with de-duplicated e-mail alerts. /etc/nhc/nhc.conf The config. The shipped one is a catalogue of examples , not a working config. /etc/nhc/scripts/ .nhc Check modules ( common.nhc , lbnl fs.nhc , lbnl hw.nhc , lanl nvgpu.nhc , ...). Only files ending in .nhc are loaded. /usr/libexec/nhc/node-mark-offline , node-mark-online Helpers that talk to Slurm/PBS/SGE/LSF. /etc/sysconfig/nhc (RHEL) or /etc/default/nhc (Debian-ish) Optional "early" settings sourced before the config. /var/log/nhc.log The run log. A logrotate snippet ships with the package. /var/run/nhc/ Detached-mode result files and (1.5+) the per-context PID file. Not sure where your build put things? On 1.5: ---

secs.head: Smoke test
secs.body: Two tests, thirty seconds: The second one will probably complain (the stock config is generic). That's fine. Writing a config that fits your nodes is part 3. [!IMPORTANT] Notice the shape of that second command: options first, then VAR=value pairs . NHC reads trailing VAR=value arguments as settings, and they must come after every flag. What does make test look like when it's happy? Every module reports ok N/N and it finishes with an "All N tests passed" line. Any failure there is worth a GitHub issue, since it means something about your platform breaks NHC's assumptions. ---

secs.head: Getting it onto 500 nodes
secs.body: Installing by hand on one node is a lab exercise. In production: 1. Bake the package into the node image (Warewulf, xCAT, Bright/BCM, OpenHPC recipes, or your golden image pipeline). The binary rarely changes. 2. Manage the config separately with your config-management tool, because the config changes often. Keep nhc.conf and any custom .nhc modules in Git. 3. Pin the version. Treat an NHC upgrade like any other change: read the release notes (1.5 has a breaking change in check file stat option letters), test on a few nodes, then roll. A minimal Ansible sketch: How to roll the config out without draining the whole cluster by accident has its own page: part 5. Takeaway: use the release tarball or RPM (never GitHub's auto "Source code" archives), run make test , put the package in the image and the config in Git.
