secs.body: - NHC README: Installation and Testing - NHC releases - UCL-ARC fork: building RPMs with make dist + rpmbuild -ta

label: 3. Writing nhc.conf
title: Writing nhc.conf That Actually Fits Your Cluster
desc: Part 3 of the Node Health Check series. The config is your health policy. This is where NHC stops being a tool and start

secs.head: Writing nhc.conf That Actually Fits Your Cluster
secs.body: Part 3 of the Node Health Check series. The config is your health policy. This is where NHC stops being a tool and starts being your bouncer.

secs.head: Anatomy of a line
secs.body: - target : which hosts run this line (a match string , next section). - : the separator. Yes, it looks like a shell "or". It isn't one here. - check : any shell command that returns success or failure. In practice, an NHC check function such as check fs mount rw . Lines are read top to bottom; the ones whose target matches the node's hostname are queued and executed in order . Order matters twice: variable assignments must come before the checks that use them, and by default the first failing check ends the run, so put cheap, high-signal checks first. ---

secs.head: Match strings: who runs what
secs.body: NHC's "match string" syntax shows up everywhere (targets, process names, mount sources, command output), so learn it once: Form Delimiters Example Matches ------ ----------- --------- --------- Glob none cn cn001 , cn-gpu7 Regex /.../ /^gpu[0-9]{3}$/ gpu001 … gpu999 Node range {...} {cn[001-128],gpu[01-16]} Slurm-style hostlists External (1.4.2+) your choice, e.g. <... <gpu-nodes whatever your helper command says Negated leading ! !login everything except login nodes [!WARNING] Node ranges in NHC are simpler than Slurm's. Only one bracketed range per name, no commas inside brackets. {cn[001-010,015]} is invalid; write {cn[001-010],cn015} . The target is matched against $HOSTNAME , which NHC reads from the kernel. If your nodes report FQDNs ( cn001.cluster.local ), your globs need to account for that, or match on the short name with a regex like /^cn0[0-9]+\./ . ---

secs.head: Let the machine write the first draft: nhc-genconf
secs.body: Counting sockets and kilobytes by hand is a fine way to waste an afternoon. nhc-genconf (1.4.1+) scans the node with the same code NHC uses and writes /etc/nhc/nhc.conf.auto : On a heterogeneous cluster, run it everywhere and let ClusterShell group identical results, which shows you your hardware classes in one screen: Each block of identical output is one hardware class. Turn each into a node-range target, and the odd node out (the one with 3 DIMMs short of its siblings) just introduced itself. [!CAUTION] nhc-genconf records what the node has , not what it should have . If you generate the config on a node with a dead DIMM, you've just declared the dead DIMM normal. Generate on a few known-good nodes per class and compare. ---

secs.head: Variables, and the precedence trap
secs.body: Settings are plain shell variables, and you can set them in three places: 1. Command line , as trailing VAR=value arguments ( nhc -d MARK OFFLINE=0 ). 2. sysconfig file : /etc/sysconfig/nhc (RHEL) or /etc/default/nhc (Debian-ish), sourced early. 3. The config file , with the normal line syntax: export VAR=value . Two traps catch nearly everyone: Trap 1: the config file beats the command line. Unlike almost every other CLI tool, a value set in nhc.conf is not overridden by VAR=value on the command line, because of how bash initializes things. If you want a command-line override to win, only apply your site value when the variable still holds NHC's built-in default (99 for MAX SYS UID ): Why if ... fi and not the shorter [[ ... ]] && ... ? Every config line is executed as a check. When the test is false, the && form returns non-zero, and NHC counts that as a failed check . Congratulations, you just drained a healthy node with a variable assignment. The cleaner habit: keep site-wide defaults in the sysconfig file, and keep nhc.conf for checks plus per-host tweaks. Trap 2: some variables are "early" only. TIMEOUT , CONFFILE , DETACHED MODE , LOGFILE , NAME , HOSTNAME and a few others don't work from the config file . By the time the config line runs, the watchdog is already armed or the file already open. Put them in the sysconfig file or on the command line. A good /etc/sysconfig/nhc : ---

secs.head: The checks you'll actually use
secs.body: NHC ships dozens of checks. These cover 90% of real configs: Area Check Example ------ ------- --------- Filesystems check fs mount rw / check fs mount ro check fs mount rw -t nfs -s 'nas01:/export/home' -f /home check fs free , check fs used , check fs ifree check fs free /tmp 10% CPU / memory check hw cpuinfo sockets cores threads check hw cpuinfo 2 128 128 check hw physmem min max [fudge] check hw physmem 512GB 512GB 3% check hw mcelog needs mcelog ; newer distros use rasdaemon instead Network check hw ib rate [device] check hw ib 400 mlx5 0 (NDR) check hw eth , check net link (1.5) check net link eno1 check net ping check net ping -W 2 -c 2 slurmctl01 Processes check ps service check ps service -u root -S sshd check ps unauth users , check ps userproc lineage catch stray user processes not started by slurmd check ps loadavg check ps loadavg '' 300 GPUs check nvsmi healthmon , check nvgpu smi (1.5) wraps nvidia-smi Anything check cmd output , check cmd status , check file contents turn any command into a check Sizes take suffixes ( kB , MB , GB , TB ) and the memory checks accept a fudge factor . Use it: the kernel never reports exactly the RAM on the invoice, and firmware updates shift it by a few MB. [!TIP] On nodes that mount NFS or Lustre, set DF FLAGS="-Tkal" (and DFI FLAGS="-Tial" ) before any check fs free / check fs used lines. The -l makes df skip network filesystems, so a dead NFS server can't hang your local-disk checks. Upstream calls this strongly recommended . ---

secs.head: Starter config: a real cluster
secs.body: A fictional but realistic cluster: 512 CPU nodes cn001-512 , 32 GPU nodes gpu01-32 (8 GPUs, NDR InfiniBand each), two login nodes. Adjust the numbers to your hardware; keep the structure. Notes on the choices: - Section 1 runs first because if / is read-only or sshd is dead, nothing else matters. - check ps service -S restarts a missing daemon and fails the check, so the node drains now and comes back on the next clean run. That's auto-remediation in one flag; part 7 goes deeper. - Swap pinned to zero catches the node that booted the wrong image with a swap partition. - The Xid line fails if the kernel log contains the listed, hardware-flavored NVIDIA Xid codes (double-bit ECC, fallen off the bus and friends). Xids stay in dmesg until reboot, which is what you want here: these need a reset anyway. Tune the list to your GPUs and NVIDIA's current Xid catalogue. Part 6 builds richer GPU checks. - The rogue-process checks only log at first. Switch to kill only after you've watched the logs for a week and trust them. ---

secs.head: Contexts: one binary, many personalities
secs.body: A context is a named configuration. The name comes from how NHC was invoked (default: nhc ), and it decides which files load: Invocation Config file sysconfig file ----------- ------------- ---------------- nhc /etc/nhc/nhc.conf /etc/sysconfig/nhc nhc -n nhc-epilog /etc/nhc/nhc-epilog.conf /etc/sysconfig/nhc-epilog nhc-deep (a symlink to nhc ) /etc/nhc/nhc-deep.conf /etc/sysconfig/nhc-deep A tidy layout for the "four moments" from part 1: - nhc.conf : periodic, well under a minute. - nhc-epilog.conf : a handful of seconds; "did that job leave a mess?" - nhc-deep.conf : minutes are fine; DCGM level 2, memory tests, IB bandwidth. ---

secs.head: Iterate until silent
secs.body: The loop that turns a draft into a production config: - -a runs all checks and returns the number that failed. - -v prints each check (with its number, on 1.5) as it runs. - -l- sends log output to the terminal instead of /var/log/nhc.log . On 1.5 you can even test another node's config lines from your desk with -m host (masquerade): nhc -a -v -l- -m gpu07 MARK OFFLINE=0 . The checks still run against this machine's hardware, so treat it as a "which lines apply to gpu07?" tool, not a remote health check. Each failure is either a config bug (your expectation is wrong; fix the line) or a node bug (the node is wrong; fix the node). Telling those apart across a whole fleet is what part 5 is about. But first, let's plug NHC into Slurm in part 4. Takeaway: order checks cheap-to-expensive, generate a draft with nhc-genconf on known-good nodes, keep "early" variables in the sysconfig file, and iterate with nhc -a -v -l- MARK OFFLINE=0 until it's silent.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NHC README: Configuration, Match Strings, Contexts, Built-in Checks - Sample nhc.conf shipped upstream - NVIDIA Xid errors catalogue

label: 4. Slurm integration
title: Plugging NHC into Slurm (and Friends)
desc: Part 4 of the Node Health Check series. NHC knows how to judge a node. Now we give it a schedule, a timeout that won't g

secs.head: Plugging NHC into Slurm (and Friends)
secs.body: Part 4 of the Node Health Check series. NHC knows how to judge a node. Now we give it a schedule, a timeout that won't get it killed mid-sentence, and the right to drain.

secs.head: The three lines
secs.body: Add to slurm.conf on every node and the controller (Slurm expects the file identical everywhere, even though only slurmd runs the program): Then tell NHC which resource manager it's talking to, in /etc/sysconfig/nhc (or /etc/default/nhc ): NHC can auto-detect Slurm, but pinning it removes one variable from every future debugging session. Apply the Slurm side with scontrol reconfigure (or restart slurmctld and the slurmd s), and confirm: What each line does: Setting Meaning Advice --------- --------- -------- HealthCheckProgram Absolute path, run as root by slurmd Point at nhc directly, or at a tiny wrapper if you need flags HealthCheckInterval Seconds between runs. Default 0 = never 300 is the classic value. Go to 3600 if users report jitter HealthCheckNodeState Which node states get checked (next section) ANY,CYCLE is a sane default Want to pass flags? Use a wrapper, because HealthCheckProgram takes a path, not a command line: ---

secs.head: Which nodes should get checked? HealthCheckNodeState
secs.body: Value Runs on Typical use ------- --------- ------------- ANY (default) Every node, busy or not Catch problems even under running jobs IDLE Idle nodes (drained-and-idle included) Jitter-sensitive sites NONDRAINED IDLE (23.02+) Idle nodes that are not drained See the warning below ALLOC / MIXED Fully / partially allocated nodes Rare on their own; combine with others CYCLE Combine with the above: spreads runs across the interval instead of all at once Big clusters, shared filesystems START ONLY Only when slurmd starts Boot-time validation only REBOOT ONLY Only when slurmd reports back after a reboot Post-reboot validation only START ONLY and REBOOT ONLY can't be combined with anything else. [!WARNING] NONDRAINED IDLE breaks NHC's auto-resume. NHC brings a node back by passing a later check, but this state means drained nodes are never checked again. Every NHC drain becomes a manual resume. That can be exactly what you want (human eyes on every failure) but choose it on purpose. Why CYCLE ? Without it, all 2,000 nodes run NHC in the same second. If your checks touch NFS or Lustre (stat a file, df a mount), that's a synchronized thundering herd against your metadata server every five minutes. CYCLE staggers them. ---

secs.head: Timeouts: make sure the bouncer isn't shot mid-sentence
secs.body: There are two clocks, and they need to agree: Clock Default Who sets it ------- --------- ------------- NHC watchdog TIMEOUT 30 s /etc/sysconfig/nhc or -t Slurm kills the program 60 s ( HealthCheckTimeout on recent Slurm, max 65535) slurm.conf Rule: NHC's timeout must be shorter than Slurm's. When NHC's watchdog fires, NHC reports a clean "timed out" failure and drains with a reason. When Slurm's fires first, NHC just dies silently, nothing gets drained, and you learn nothing. What if your checks genuinely need minutes (GPU stress, bandwidth tests)? Don't stretch the periodic timeout. Pick one: 1. Move them to a deep context run from cron or by your remediation loop (part 7). 2. Detached mode ( DETACHED MODE=1 in sysconfig): NHC forks, returns the previous run's result immediately, and runs the checks in the background. slurmd never blocks. The catch: a fresh failure is only acted on at the next run, so a job can land on a node that broke five minutes ago. [!NOTE] On your Slurm version, man slurm.conf is the truth: older releases have a fixed 60-second kill and no HealthCheckTimeout knob. ---

secs.head: Life of a failure, end to end
secs.body: Let's break cn042 on purpose (on a test node, please): Within one HealthCheckInterval , slurmd runs NHC, check fs mount rw fails, and the offline helper runs the equivalent of: From the controller (the exact wording depends on the check and NHC version): Running jobs keep running (the node is DRAINING, then DRAINED). No new jobs land. Now fix it: Next run, every check passes, the online helper sees a reason starting with NHC: , and resumes the node. Zero humans paged. That's the whole point. ---

secs.head: Draining etiquette for humans
secs.body: Because of the NHC: handshake from part 1: Two more NHC 1.5 behaviors worth knowing: - Nodes in Slurm's MAINT state are never resumed by NHC (Slurm rejects that transition anyway). - Run with -p and NHC marks failures as permanent : the reason gets a (perm) tag and NHC won't resume it, ever. Good for hardware classes where any failure means an RMA. ---

secs.head: Boot and reboot: the sneaky part
secs.body: slurmd runs the health check when it starts, before it registers with the controller . A failing check at boot means the node doesn't register as healthy. That's great when the check is right and baffling when your config is wrong (see troubleshooting). Reboots via scontrol reboot used to be a mess: Slurm clears the DRAIN flag when a node comes back from an ASAP reboot, which could wipe out what the health check had decided. NHC 1.5 merged a set of fixes for this (PR 115 by Trey Dockendorf). After a plain scontrol reboot , the helper keeps the node drained until NHC itself onlines it, and it no longer fights the Reboot ASAP reason. If you reboot nodes from automation, run 1.5 . ---

secs.head: Prolog and Epilog: checks at job boundaries
secs.body: The periodic check has a blind spot: the five minutes between runs. Job boundaries close it. Epilog: "did that job break the node?" Jobs leave /tmp full, orphan processes behind, or trigger GPU errors. A short epilog check catches it before the next job lands: Prolog: "is it safe to start?" Here you want a non-zero exit. When a prolog fails, Slurm drains the node and requeues the job instead of letting it die: [!CAUTION] Every second in the prolog/epilog is a second added to every job. A 30-second epilog on a cluster doing 100,000 short jobs a day burns 830 node-hours of idle time. Keep these contexts tiny: mounts, GPU count, a dmesg Xid grep, done. ---

secs.head: Not on Slurm? PBS, Grid Engine, cron, Kubernetes
secs.body: PBS / TORQUE ( mom priv/config on each MOM): That runs every 5 MOM intervals plus at job start and end. For NHC to offline nodes with notes, the nodes need operator rights: qmgr -c "set server operators += root@ " . The NHC: note rule works the same as in Slurm. Grid Engine family : follow Dave Love's SGE NHC recipe, which upstream points to. LSF : supported ("sorta", in upstream's own words) via badmin hclose / hopen . Plain cron , for servers with no scheduler (storage nodes, login nodes), use nhc-wrapper . It de-duplicates results, so you get one e-mail when a problem appears, one when it clears, and a reminder while it persists: Kubernetes : NHC 1.5 ships check kube checks, and Azure documents a pattern that runs AzNHC in an init container and taints the node ( NoExecute ) on failure, the k8s equivalent of a drain. Next up: getting this onto hundreds of nodes without draining all of them on the first run, in part 5. Takeaway: three slurm.conf lines plus NHC RM=slurm ; keep NHC's timeout under Slurm's; use CYCLE on big clusters; never drain without a reason; run 1.5 if you reboot nodes from automation.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - slurm.conf : HealthCheckProgram / Interval / NodeState / Timeout - NHC README: Slurm, TORQUE, Grid Engine integration, periodic execution, detached mode - NHC 1.5 release notes (Slurm reboot handling, MAINT, -p ) - Slurm: Prolog and Epilog guide - Azure: Pre-job health checks on AKS

label: 5. Rolling out to a fleet
title: Rolling NHC Out to a Fleet Without Draining Everything
desc: Part 5 of the Node Health Check series. A config typo in nhc.conf is the fastest way to take a 2,000-node cluster to zer

secs.head: Rolling NHC Out to a Fleet Without Draining Everything
secs.body: Part 5 of the Node Health Check series. A config typo in nhc.conf is the fastest way to take a 2,000-node cluster to zero. Here's how to make that impossible, or at least boring.

secs.head: The failure mode we're designing against
secs.body: You push a config with check hw physmem 512GB 512GB and no fudge factor. The kernel on every node reports 503 GB. Within five minutes, every node in the partition is drain with NHC: check hw physmem: ... . Running jobs finish; nothing new starts. Your queue grows; your phone rings. Health checks are a fleet-wide kill switch you hand to a config file. Treat changes to that file like production deployments, because they are. The plan below works for the first NHC rollout and for every config change after it. ---

secs.head: Phase 0: inventory
secs.body: Know your hardware classes before writing expectations about them: clush -b folds identical output together, so each block is one hardware class with its node list. Three blocks where you expected one? You just found the nodes with a missing DIMM or a BIOS that disabled hyperthreading. Write the config from the majority of each class (part 3). ---

secs.head: Phase 1: dry run, fleet-wide
secs.body: Install the package and config everywhere, but don't set HealthCheckProgram yet. Run NHC by hand, in check-all mode, with draining disabled: - -a reports every failure, not just the first. - -l- prints to stdout so clush can collect it. - MARK OFFLINE=0 guarantees nothing gets drained. Healthy nodes print nothing. With -b , failing nodes collapse into groups by identical message, so 2,000 nodes of output become a dozen readable blocks. [!TIP] Run the dry run twice , at different times of day. Checks like check ps loadavg and check fs free behave very differently at 3 AM and during the 10 AM job storm. ---

secs.head: Phase 2: triage, config bug or node bug?
secs.body: For each block of failures, ask one question: If the failure is on... It's probably... Do this ------------------------- ------------------ --------- All (or most) nodes of a class A config bug : your expectation is wrong Fix the line: add a fudge factor, correct the count, fix the target A handful of nodes A node bug : those nodes really are different Fix the nodes, or drain them yourself with a human reason Random nodes, changing each run A flaky check Make it more robust (retries, tolerance) or drop it Iterate until the dry run is quiet except for nodes that are really broken and that you've consciously drained. ---

secs.head: Phase 3: canary, enforcing on a few nodes
secs.body: slurm.conf must be identical on all nodes, so you can't enable HealthCheckProgram on just 16 of them. Instead, enable it everywhere and do the canary inside nhc.conf , since lines run in order and later assignments win: Now every node runs every check and logs failures, but only cn001-016 can actually drain. Leave it a few days. Watch /var/log/nhc.log across the fleet and sinfo -R on the canaries. Then widen: {cn[001-128]} , then delete both lines. ---

secs.head: Phase 4: enforce everywhere, with a circuit breaker
secs.body: Even with a perfect rollout, a future change will eventually go wrong. Add a circuit breaker : something outside NHC that notices when "too many" nodes are NHC-drained, and screams. What should happen when it trips? At minimum, a page. Bolder sites also flip a kill switch: push export MARK OFFLINE=0 to the top of nhc.conf cluster-wide, so NHC keeps logging but stops draining until a human looks. [!WARNING] Don't make the breaker auto-resume nodes. If 30% of your nodes really did lose Lustre, resuming them recreates 600 black holes at once. Stop new drains; let a human decide about existing ones. ---

secs.head: Day two: logs, metrics and config changes
secs.body: Config lives in Git. Every change gets a pull request and a one-line "why". When a node drains on Tuesday, git log -p nhc.conf tells you whether Monday's change did it. Every config change replays phases 1 to 3 in miniature: dry run the new file on the fleet without installing it (process substitution works for -c in 1.5), then canary. Logs. /var/log/nhc.log on each node (logrotate snippet included), failures also to syslog. NHC 1.5 can format syslog messages as JSON ( -j , or NHC FMT JSON=1 ), which your log pipeline (Loki, Elastic, Splunk) will parse without regex sorcery. Metrics worth graphing: - Count of nodes with an NHC: reason, over time (the circuit breaker's number). - Top 10 NHC failure messages this week. The top one is your next hardware conversation or config fix. - Time from NHC drain to resume. Long tails mean manual work you could automate (part 7). A crude exporter is ten lines: sinfo -h -N -R -o '%E' piped into a textfile for node exporter's textfile collector. ---

secs.head: Jitter: the "NHC slowed my job" conversation
secs.body: Sooner or later, someone running a tightly coupled MPI code will ask whether NHC is stealing their cycles. Upstream designed NHC to keep "OS jitter" minimal (bash builtins, few forks) and reports no significant jitter in practice, including on very sensitive systems. If it is a concern on your cluster, upstream's own suggestions: 1. Raise HealthCheckInterval from 300 to 3600 seconds. 2. Use HealthCheckNodeState=IDLE (or NONDRAINED IDLE , knowing the trade-off) so busy nodes aren't checked. 3. Have heavier checks skip or slim down when a job is running on the node, and rely on the epilog to cover job boundaries. Measure before and after with the user's actual code. Feelings are not a benchmark. Takeaway: dry run with -a -l- MARK OFFLINE=0 across the fleet, triage config bugs vs node bugs, canary with MARK OFFLINE inside nhc.conf , then enforce behind a circuit breaker. Every config change after that repeats the cycle.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NHC README: Testing, Periodic Execution and the jitter note - NHC 1.5 release notes (JSON syslog, PID file, config from pipes) - ClusterShell documentation

label: 6. Custom checks
title: Writing Your Own NHC Checks
desc: Part 6 of the Node Health Check series. The built-in checks cover the classics. Your cluster has its own weirdness: a li

secs.head: Writing Your Own NHC Checks
secs.body: Part 6 of the Node Health Check series. The built-in checks cover the classics. Your cluster has its own weirdness: a licence daemon, a GPU generation with its own failure modes, a burst buffer. Time to teach the bouncer some new rules.

secs.head: First, do you even need a module?
secs.body: Often no. check cmd output , check cmd status and check file contents turn almost any command or file into a check with no code at all: check cmd output passes when every positive -m match is found and no negated one is. Each -M gives the matching -m a readable failure message, and -C name makes the failure show up under a name of your choice. In 1.5 it also gained conditionals ( -c ), so you can compare numbers from the output, not just match text. Write a module when you need logic : loops over devices, thresholds per device, cached data shared between several checks. ---

secs.head: The rules of the house
secs.body: From upstream's guidelines, plus what bites people in practice: 1. File: /etc/nhc/scripts/<siteid <class .nhc , for example acme gpu.nhc . The .nhc extension is required ; other files are ignored (so .rpmnew leftovers don't get loaded). 2. Function names: check <class <purpose , like check gpu count . Helpers: nhc <class gather data . 3. Namespace your globals: ACME GPU ... , never DATA or COUNT . Every module shares one bash process. 4. Fail with die : die 1 "clear message" then return 1 . The message becomes the NHC: reason in sinfo -R , so make it say what and where : "GPU 3 (0000:3b:00.0): 12 uncorrected ECC errors" beats "gpu bad" . 5. Pass with return 0 . Silence is success. 6. Cache expensive data in a gather function, so three checks don't run nvidia-smi three times. 7. Bound every external command with a timeout. A wedged GPU can hang nvidia-smi forever; NHC's watchdog will eventually kill the whole run , with a much less useful message than yours. 8. Use full paths or extend PATH . NHC runs with PATH=/sbin:/usr/sbin:/bin:/usr/bin , not your login shell's. ---

secs.head: Skeleton: a module in five parts
secs.body: Parts 4 and 5 live elsewhere: the line in nhc.conf ( check acme thing ok ) and a test run (below). ---

secs.head: Real example: GPU count and ECC errors
secs.body: The most common GPU failure modes in production are boringly physical: a GPU falls off the bus (count drops from 8 to 7) or memory errors pile up. Here's a module that catches both from one nvidia-smi call. And in nhc.conf : Design notes: - One gather, two checks. The second check reuses the cached rows. - Fails loudly when nvidia-smi itself fails. A driver that can't talk to the GPUs is a failure, not "zero GPUs, zero errors, all good". - Volatile vs aggregate counters. Volatile counters reset with the driver; aggregate ones persist. Which one to alert on, and at what threshold, depends on your GPU generation's error-recovery features (row remapping and friends). Read NVIDIA's guidance for your hardware and adjust the field name. - Field names change between driver versions. Check nvidia-smi --help-query-gpu on your nodes before trusting this verbatim. Pair it with the dmesg Xid one-liner from part 3, and you have count, memory errors and kernel-reported faults covered in milliseconds. ---

secs.head: Real example: wrapping DCGM
secs.body: NVIDIA's DCGM offers two very different kinds of checks, and they belong in different places: DCGM feature Cost Where it belongs -------------- ------ ------------------ Background health ( dcgmi health -c after watches are set with dcgmi health -s ) Cheap, non-invasive Periodic NHC run Active diagnostics ( dcgmi diag -r 1/2/3/4 ) Level 1 takes seconds, level 2 about two minutes, level 3 about fifteen, level 4 longer; levels 2+ load the GPUs Never periodic. Deep context, after a drain, or burn-in NVIDIA's own guidance maps the levels to jobs: level 1 as a readiness check, level 2 after failures, levels 3-4 for administrators doing a post-mortem. A check that runs the quick diagnostic and fails on any failing test: Because it reuses check cmd output , it inherits the timeout, the exit-code check and the matching for free. Wire it into the deep context, not the periodic one: The deep context needs a watchdog longer than its slowest check, so give it its own early settings, for example TIMEOUT=900 in /etc/sysconfig/nhc-deep . The periodic context keeps its short timeout. [!IMPORTANT] DCGM's output format and exit codes evolve between releases, and newer releases can emit JSON ( -j ). Run dcgmi diag -r 1 on a known-bad and a known-good node, confirm what "fail" looks like on your version, and adjust the match. NHC 1.5 also ships GPU checks of its own ( lanl nvgpu.nhc for nvidia-smi, csc nvidia smi.nhc ), so read those first; they may already do what you need. ---

secs.head: Testing your check
secs.body: Remember the ordering rule from part 2: flags first, VAR=value pairs last. Also run these as a real root shell rather than through sudo , which closes extra file descriptors like the 33 used for the trace. Step 4 is the one people skip. A check that has never failed in testing is a check you don't know works. [!TIP] To fake a failure without breaking hardware, point the command variable at a stub: ACME NVSMI=/tmp/fake-nvidia-smi (a script that prints 7 rows or a non-zero ECC count). This is why the module reads ACME NVSMI instead of hardcoding the path. ---

secs.head: Writing bash like NHC does
secs.body: NHC is fast because it avoids forking subprocesses. Your checks run on every node every few minutes, so the same habits pay off: Instead of Write Why ----------- ------- ----- X=$(cat /proc/loadavg) read -a X < /proc/loadavg read is a builtin: no fork HOST=$(hostname) read HOST < /proc/sys/kernel/hostname Same, and NHC already sets $HOSTNAME cmd \ grep foo [[ "$LINE" == foo ]] or [[ "$LINE" =~ regex ]] Matching in-process echo "$S" \ sed 's/^ //' ${S "${S%%[! ] }"} Parameter expansion awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd while IFS=: read -r U ; do ...; done < /etc/passwd One process instead of two Three checks each calling the tool One gather function + cached array The tool runs once For matching, call NHC's own mcheck "$string" "$match string" so your check accepts globs, /regex/ , {ranges} and !negation just like the built-ins. ---

secs.head: Sharing upstream
secs.body: Wrote something others would want (a check for a common NIC, filesystem or GPU)? Upstream welcomes pull requests. Include the header comment, keep the naming convention, and add unit tests under test/ like the existing modules. Several of the GPU and Kubernetes checks in 1.5 started life as exactly that kind of site module (LANL, CSC). Next: turning "detected" into "fixed" without turning your cluster into a reboot loop, in part 7. Takeaway: try check cmd output first; write a module when you need logic. Namespace globals, cache expensive data, bound every command with a timeout, write failure messages a human can act on, and prove each check fails when it should.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NHC README: Customization, Writing Checks, Tips and Best Practices - NHC check cmd output documentation - NVIDIA DCGM diagnostics: run levels - dcgmi diag command reference

label: 7. Auto-remediation
title: Auto-Remediation: From Detected to Fixed, Safely
desc: Part 7 of the Node Health Check series. Draining a sick node is defense. This page is offense: fixing the boring 80% of

secs.head: Auto-Remediation: From Detected to Fixed, Safely
secs.body: Part 7 of the Node Health Check series. Draining a sick node is defense. This page is offense: fixing the boring 80% of failures without a human, while making sure automation never turns one bad node into a hundred.

secs.head: The loop
secs.body: Every good remediation system, from a 50-node lab cluster to a hyperscaler's GPU fleet, runs the same loop: The key insight: NHC already does half of this. It detects, it drains with a reason, and it re-verifies and resumes on its next run. All you need to add is the "fix" step, plus rules about when to stop trying. ---

secs.head: The escalation ladder
secs.body: Not every failure deserves the same response. Climb one rung at a time: Rung Action Example failures Who acts ------ -------- ------------------ ---------- 0. Fix in place Restart a daemon, remount a filesystem munged died, NFS mount dropped NHC itself, during the check 1. Clean reboot Drain, wait for jobs to finish, reboot GPU Xid 79, leaked memory, stuck D-state processes Node doctor 2. Deep verify After reboot, run slow diagnostics before resuming ECC errors, flaky IB link Node doctor + deep context 3. Human / RMA Ticket, keep drained with a non-NHC reason Same failure after reboot, DIMM missing, hardware inventory changed People The rule of thumb: automate what's cheap to get wrong. Restarting munged on a healthy node costs nothing. Rebooting a node with a running 3-day job costs a lot. ---

secs.head: Rung 0: fix in place with NHC's own flags
secs.body: Several built-in checks take a fix action. The pattern is always the same: the check still fails this run (so the node drains), the fix runs in the background, and the next run passes and resumes the node. The useful flags: Check Flag Effect ------- ------ -------- check ps service -S / -r / -c start / restart / stop-then-start the service if not running -e cmd / -E cmd run cmd if the process is missing / present -s / -k stop / kill a service that shouldn't be running check fs mount -r mount -o remount options in the background -e cmd / -E cmd run cmd if missing / found check ps cpu , check ps mem , check ps time -r N / -k / -K renice / kill the process / kill its parent check net socket -e cmd run cmd if the expected socket isn't there Most checks -0 non-fatal : log the problem, don't drain [!TIP] The fix runs as root, from NHC, under slurmd . Make fix scripts idempotent, quick and quiet, and give them full paths. If your fix needs more than a few seconds, it's not a rung-0 fix; hand it to the node doctor. ---

secs.head: What you must never auto-fix
secs.body: Automation that hides problems is worse than no automation. Keep your hands off: - Anything that kills user processes on a node running jobs. With HealthCheckNodeState=ANY , check ps unauth users kill or check ps mem -k can terminate a legitimate job if your "authorized" logic has a gap. Log first ( log syslog ), watch for weeks, then decide. - Resetting error counters (GPU ECC, IB port counters, mcelog ) to make a check pass. You just erased the evidence the vendor will ask for. - Recurring failures. A node that needed a reboot three times this week is broken hardware wearing a fake moustache. That's rung 3. - Anything during a cluster-wide event. If 20% of nodes fail the same check at once, the problem is shared (fabric, filesystem, a bad config push). Rebooting 400 nodes makes it worse. That's the circuit breaker's job (part 5). ---

secs.head: Rungs 1-2: the node doctor
secs.body: Rebooting and deep diagnostics don't belong inside NHC: they're slow, and a node can't reliably reboot itself in the middle of its own health check. Run a small node doctor on the controller (or wherever you run cluster automation). It reads NHC's drain reasons, matches them against rules, and acts. Prerequisites: RebootProgram set in slurm.conf (so scontrol reboot works), and NHC 1.5 on the nodes so post-reboot drain handling is correct (part 4). [!WARNING] No ASAP , no nextstate= here. Per the scontrol docs, Slurm clears the node's DRAIN flag after an ASAP reboot or one with nextstate=resume / down . The node would rejoin the pool as soon as slurmd registers, without waiting for your verification. Since NHC has already drained the node, a plain scontrol reboot is all you need. How the loop closes: 1. NHC drains gpu07 with NHC: ... Xid ... 79 ... . 2. The doctor matches the Xid, records the attempt, and runs scontrol reboot gpu07 . Running jobs finish first; the drain keeps new ones away. 3. gpu07 reboots. slurmd runs NHC at startup, and NHC 1.5 keeps a freshly rebooted node drained until NHC itself onlines it. 4. Checks pass; the reason still starts with NHC: , so NHC resumes the node. Nobody woke up. 5. If it happens again within 24 hours, the doctor tries one more reboot. The third time, it rewrites the reason without the NHC: prefix. Thanks to the handshake, NHC will now never auto-resume it: it's a human's node. Adding rung 2 (deep verify). For failures like ECC errors, a clean boot isn't proof enough. Before rebooting, the doctor claims the node with its own reason, so NHC won't resume it after the reboot: On a later round, once the node is back up, it runs the deep context and hands ownership back: Handing a node back with an NHC: reason is the neat trick here: you never call scontrol update state=resume from automation; NHC does it, only after its own checks pass. [!NOTE] This is deliberately a ~60-line script, not a platform. It's enough for most clusters. Big GPU fleets often grow this into a proper service (a state machine with a database, vendor ticket integration, dashboards); the rules and guard rails stay the same. ---

secs.head: Guard rails, or how not to reboot the whole cluster
secs.body: The script above already has the four that matter most. Don't remove them: Guard rail Prevents ----------- ---------- Dry-run default Learning how your regex behaves on production data the hard way Retry budget per node ( MAX ATTEMPTS in WINDOW SECS ) Infinite reboot loops on genuinely broken hardware Concurrency limit ( MAX CONCURRENT ) A shared failure turning into a mass reboot Allowlist of failure types ( REBOOTABLE ) Rebooting for problems a reboot can't fix (wrong RAM size, missing DIMM) Plus two operational ones: - Every action is logged with node, reason and attempt number. When someone asks "why did gpu07 reboot at 03:12?", the answer is in syslog. - Pair it with the circuit breaker. If the breaker trips, the doctor stops. A shared outage is a human's problem. ---

secs.head: Rung 3: hand off to humans and vendors
secs.body: When automation gives up, make the handoff useful: - A reason that tells the story : ESCALATED: Xid 79 on GPU 3 after 2 reboots (doctor gave up) beats bad . - Evidence collected before anyone touches it : dmesg , nvidia-smi -q , ipmitool sel list , the last nhc.log lines, a nvidia-bug-report.sh for GPUs. Vendors ask for these first; collect them automatically into the ticket. - NHC's permanent mode for hardware classes where any failure means RMA: run those nodes' NHC with -p (1.5) and failures are tagged (perm) , never auto-resumed. ---

secs.head: Notifications without the spam
secs.body: Nobody reads the 400th identical e-mail. Two NHC-native tools help: - nhc-wrapper for cron-driven contexts: it compares each run with the previous one and only reports changes , plus a reminder every -X interval while a problem persists: - JSON syslog ( -j , 1.5) into your log pipeline, with alerting rules on rates ("more than 5 new NHC drains in 15 minutes") rather than individual events. Page humans for escalations and breaker trips . Everything else is a dashboard. Next, when things don't behave: part 8, troubleshooting. Takeaway: NHC already detects, drains, re-verifies and resumes. Add fixes in place with -S , -r , -e , and a small node doctor for reboots, guarded by dry-run, retry budgets, concurrency limits and an allowlist. When automation gives up, drop the NHC: prefix so a human owns the node.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NHC README: check ps service , check fs mount , resource checks - scontrol reboot (ASAP, nextstate, reason) - NHC 1.5 release notes: -p permanent offline, JSON syslog - NVIDIA DCGM diagnostics: which level to use when

label: 8. Troubleshooting
title: NHC Troubleshooting: Symptom First
desc: Part 8 of the Node Health Check series. Find your symptom, follow the steps. Bookmark this one; future you at 2 AM will

secs.head: NHC Troubleshooting: Symptom First
secs.body: Part 8 of the Node Health Check series. Find your symptom, follow the steps. Bookmark this one; future you at 2 AM will be grateful.

secs.head: The debugging toolkit
secs.body: Memorize these five; they solve most problems. ---

secs.head: 1. A healthy node keeps getting drained
secs.body: Look at the reason first. sinfo -R -n <node usually names the check. Then rerun with -a -v -l- MARK OFFLINE=0 on the node. Likely cause Tell-tale Fix ------------- ----------- ----- Expectation is wrong for this hardware class Same failure on all nodes of a class Fix the config line or its target (part 3) Memory check without fudge factor check hw physmem complaining by a few hundred MB Add a fudge: check hw physmem 512GB 512GB 3% Threshold checks during busy hours check ps loadavg , check fs free fail only by day Raise thresholds, or move them to a non-draining context Flaky network check check net ping fails randomly More packets and a longer wait ( -c 3 -W 3 ); check the target isn't overloaded Target matches more hosts than intended Login nodes failing compute checks Test with nhc -m login01 -a -v -l- MARK OFFLINE=0 (1.5) to see which lines apply Hostname format mismatch Checks for cn not running, or running for the wrong nodes Compare cat /proc/sys/kernel/hostname with your targets (FQDN vs short name) ---

secs.head: 2. The problem is fixed but the node never comes back
secs.body: NHC resumes a node only when all of these are true. Walk the list: 1. The reason still starts with NHC: . If someone (or a script) edited it, NHC no longer owns the node. sinfo -R -n <node . Fix: resume it yourself, or set the reason back to an NHC: one. 2. NHC actually runs on drained nodes. HealthCheckNodeState=NONDRAINED IDLE never checks drained nodes, so they never get resumed. scontrol show config grep -i healthcheck . 3. The node isn't in MAINT . NHC 1.5 doesn't resume nodes in maintenance state; Slurm rejects that transition anyway. 4. It wasn't a permanent failure. A (perm) tag in the reason means NHC ran with -p . Humans only. 5. MARK OFFLINE isn't 0. Left over from a canary or a dry run? It disables onlining too. grep -r MARK OFFLINE /etc/nhc /etc/sysconfig/nhc /etc/default/nhc 2 /dev/null . 6. All checks pass now , not just the one you fixed. With default settings NHC stops at the first failure, so a second, hidden problem keeps it drained. Run with -a . 7. The online helper can talk to Slurm. Look in nhc.log for helper output; scontrol must work from the node as root. ---

secs.head: 3. Node is drained, but not by NHC
secs.body: If the reason doesn't start with NHC: , NHC didn't do it, and NHC won't undo it. Common culprits: Reason Who did it -------- ----------- Kill task failed slurmd couldn't kill a job step (often processes stuck in D state on a dead filesystem) Epilog error / Prolog error Your prolog/epilog exited non-zero Not responding / NO NETWORK ADDRESS Controller lost contact with slurmd Low RealMemory / Low socket core thread count Node registered with less hardware than slurm.conf says Reboot ASAP Someone ran scontrol reboot ASAP Empty A human, being mysterious Fun fact: Kill task failed and an NHC check fs mount failure often show up together. Same root cause (dead storage), two different detectors. ---

secs.head: 4. After boot, the node never registers with Slurm
secs.body: slurmd runs the health check at startup, before registering . If NHC fails, the node stays out of the pool. Typical boot-time-only failures: - Mounts not ready yet. NFS/Lustre mount after slurmd starts. Order your units ( After=remote-fs.target in a slurmd drop-in) instead of loosening the check. - GPU driver not initialized. Persistence daemon or fabric manager not started yet. Same fix: unit ordering. - Image drift. The node booted an image whose hardware or software differs from what the config expects. [!TIP] Need the node up now while you fix the config? Temporarily run with a known-good config, nhc -c /etc/nhc/nhc.conf.minimal , via the HealthCheckProgram wrapper, rather than removing health checks cluster-wide. ---

secs.head: 5. NHC times out, or gets killed silently
secs.body: Two clocks again (part 4): - NHC's watchdog fired (default 30 s): you'll see a timeout failure in nhc.log and a drain reason saying so. Something in your checks was slow. - Slurm killed NHC (60 s, or HealthCheckTimeout ): no NHC message at all, just a truncated log. Your TIMEOUT is higher than Slurm's. Lower it. Find the slow check: The usual suspect: df hanging on a dead NFS or Lustre mount inside check fs free / check fs used / check fs inodes . Fixes, in order of preference: 1. DF FLAGS="-Tkal" and DFI FLAGS="-Tial" so df skips network filesystems when you only check local ones. 2. Check network filesystems with check fs mount (reads /proc/mounts , doesn't touch the server) instead of space checks. 3. DETACHED MODE=1 so slurmd never blocks (accepting that failures are reported one run late). Other slow spots: nvidia-smi on a wedged GPU (wrap it in timeout ), dmidecode on some BMCs, DNS lookups in check net ping (use IPs or /etc/hosts ). Two NHCs at once? NHC 1.5 keeps a per-context PID file, so a second run won't pile on top of a hung one. On older versions, overlapping runs are possible when checks run longer than the interval. ---

secs.head: 6. Works when I run it, fails under slurmd
secs.body: Your shell and slurmd 's environment are not the same: Difference Symptom Fix ----------- --------- ----- PATH (NHC sets /sbin:/usr/sbin:/bin:/usr/bin ) "command not found", exit 127 Full paths in checks, or \ \ export PATH="$PATH:/opt/x/bin" at the top of the config Environment modules / LD LIBRARY PATH Vendor tools fail to load libraries Call tools through a wrapper script that sets their environment Ran as a user vs root Permission errors on dmesg , /dev/ slurmd runs it as root; test as root too sudo closing file descriptors Your trace redirect ( 33 ) is empty Use a real root shell for tracing ---

secs.head: 7. My config change does nothing
secs.body: - Wrong file for the context. nhc -n foo reads /etc/nhc/foo.conf , not nhc.conf . Check what's loaded with nhc -V -V -V (1.5) and -v output. - Early-only variable set in the config. TIMEOUT , DETACHED MODE , LOGFILE , CONFFILE , NAME ... go in the sysconfig file or on the command line (part 3). - Config beats command line. nhc FOO=1 loses to FOO=0 in the config. - Custom module not loading. It must end in .nhc and live in /etc/nhc/scripts/ (or $INCDIR ). bash -n it for syntax errors. - Variable set after it's used. Lines execute in order; assignments must come before the checks that need them. - Old copy on the node. Your config management didn't run. md5sum /etc/nhc/nhc.conf across the fleet with clush -b . ---

secs.head: 8. Weird errors: 126, 127, "no checks", "Unsupported RM"
secs.body: Message / code Meaning Fix --------------- --------- ----- Exit 127 Command not found Full path or PATH (see 6). 1.5 explicitly points this out Exit 126 Found but not executable chmod +x , check noexec mounts Warning: check list is empty (1.5) No line's target matched this hostname Compare targets with the real hostname; test with -m Unsupported RM detected from a helper NHC couldn't tell which resource manager to talk to Set NHC RM=slurm in /etc/sysconfig/nhc check file stat options behave differently after upgrade 1.5 breaking change: -M / -m now test the file type ; permission bits moved to -P / -p Update those lines when moving to 1.5 ---

secs.head: 9. Build and install problems
secs.body: - ./configure: No such file or directory : you downloaded GitHub's auto-generated "Source code" archive. Use the lbnl-nhc-<ver .tar.xz release asset, or run ./autogen.sh first (part 2). - make test fails : something about your platform breaks an assumption (bash version, /proc layout). That's a real bug report: post the output. - Helpers not found : the --libexecdir you built with doesn't match where NHC looks. Compare nhc -V -V -V with the files on disk, or set HELPERDIR in the sysconfig file. ---

secs.head: Still stuck?
secs.body: - Search and open issues at github.com/mej/nhc/issues. Attach the -x trace file from the toolkit above, your NHC version, distro, and the relevant config lines. - The NHC users' mailing list ( nhc@lbl.gov ) and the Slurm users' list both have years of searchable answers. Takeaway: read the reason, rerun with -a -v -l- MARK OFFLINE=0 , trace with -x when lost. Most problems are one of: wrong expectation, ownership ( NHC: prefix), timeouts, df on dead NFS, or environment differences under slurmd .

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NHC README: Testing, Command-Line Invocation, Configuration Variables - NHC 1.5 release notes: exit codes 126/127, empty check list warning, PID file, check file stat change - slurm.conf : HealthCheckProgram behavior at slurmd startup

label: 9. Architecture-driven NHC
title: Architecture-Driven NHC: Generate Health Checks from Your Cluster's Definition
desc: Part 9 of the Node Health Check series. The capstone. Parts 3 to 7 taught you to write nhc.conf by hand. This part stops

secs.head: Architecture-Driven NHC: Generate Health Checks from Your Cluster's Definition
secs.body: Part 9 of the Node Health Check series. The capstone. Parts 3 to 7 taught you to write nhc.conf by hand. This part stops doing that: you describe what the cluster is , and NHC gets built from that description. Everything here was run against real NHC 1.5, and two of its bugs-in-waiting were found that way.

secs.head: Three sources of truth, zero agreement
secs.body: On a cluster that's a few years old, the same facts live in at least three places: Fact slurm.conf says nhc.conf says The hardware says ------ ------------------- ----------------- ------------------- Memory on cn001 RealMemory=530000 512GB 503 GB usable GPUs on gpu07 Gres=gpu:h100:4 (copy-paste from the test rack) 8 8 cn513-516 exist? Yes, added last month No line matches them Yes, running jobs Each row is a real failure mode. The first gets every node drained as Low RealMemory by Slurm. The second schedules jobs onto half the GPUs. The third is the scariest: four production nodes with no health checks at all , and nothing tells you, because a node that matches no line in nhc.conf just passes. Hand-written configs drift because nobody's job is to keep them in sync. So make it a machine's job. ---

secs.head: The idea: health policy as code
secs.body: Three rules make it work: 1. The YAML is the only thing humans edit. Generated files carry a "do not edit" header and a hash of their source. 2. The generator refuses to write anything inconsistent , with itself or with slurm.conf . A bad definition fails CI, not the cluster. 3. Every generated config is executed by real NHC in CI before it reaches a node. ---

secs.head: Step 1: describe the architecture
secs.body: Model what the cluster should be, at the level an architect would draw it. The example file has five sections: Section Captures Why it's separate --------- ---------- ------------------- storage Mounts: path, type, source, read-only Shared by many classes; change the NFS server in one place fabrics Link rate and the HCAs that must be up A GPU rail design has 8 HCAs; a CPU node has one roles What a node does : services, user-process hygiene Login and compute nodes can share hardware but not policy classes Hardware classes: node list, CPU, NUMA, memory, fabric, mounts, GPUs One class per distinct hardware build defaults Fudge factors, timeouts per context, ping targets Site-wide knobs A class reads like a spec sheet: How each fact becomes a check, and in which context (part 3): Architecture fact Generated check periodic epilog deep ------------------- ---------------- :--: :--: :--: mounts check fs mount rw / ro with type and source ✅ ✅ ✅ gpus.count check arch gpu count ✅ ✅ ✅ gpus.fatal xids check cmd dmesg with a negated Xid regex ✅ ✅ ✅ role services check ps service -S (self-healing, part 7) ✅ ✅ cpu check hw cpuinfo ✅ ✅ numa nodes check arch numa nodes ✅ ✅ memory + fudge check hw physmem ✅ ✅ fabric one check hw ib rate dev per HCA ✅ ✅ gpus.model check arch gpu model ✅ ✅ role user hygiene check ps unauth users , check ps userproc lineage (log only) ✅ ✅ gpus.deep diag level check arch dcgm diag ✅ Ordering inside each class is cheapest-and-most-likely-first: mounts, then GPUs, then everything else. The epilog context stops after the GPU lines because every second there is added to every job (part 4). ---

secs.head: Step 2: the generator
secs.body: It does four jobs. 1. Validate the definition. Every node in exactly one class, every referenced role, fabric and mount defined, sockets <= cores <= threads , sizes parseable, every service known to the SERVICE MAP . All problems are reported in one run, not one per attempt. 2. Cross-check slurm.conf . The generator parses NodeName lines (including NodeName=DEFAULT and \ continuations) and compares them with the architecture. Here's the real output against a slurm.conf with the three drifts from the table at the top: And against a consistent one: The coverage check is the most valuable line in the whole tool. It turns "nodes silently without health checks" from an invisible state into a failed build. 3. Translate hostlists. Slurm and NHC disagree on range syntax (part 3): NHC allows one range per name and no commas inside brackets. The generator converts: Slurm hostlist (in YAML) NHC target (generated) --- --- cn[001-480] {cn[001-480]} gpu[01-30],gpu32 {gpu[01-30],gpu32} cn[001-010,015] {cn[001-010],cn015} 4. Emit one file per context , plus a sysconfig file each, so "early" settings like TIMEOUT land where NHC actually reads them (part 3). An excerpt of the generated periodic config: It's one cluster-wide file, the way NHC was designed to be used: every node gets the same bytes and picks its own lines. ---

secs.head: Step 3: the architecture check module
secs.body: Built-in checks cover CPUs, memory, mounts and IB. acme arch.nhc adds the architecture facts NHC doesn't know about: Check Verifies ------- ---------- check arch numa nodes N NUMA nodes online, parsed from /sys/devices/system/node/online in pure bash. Catches a BIOS reset to the wrong NPS / sub-NUMA setting, a classic silent performance killer check arch gpu count N GPUs visible to nvidia-smi (timeout-bounded, cached) check arch gpu model S Every GPU's name contains S . Catches the wrong card swapped in by a well-meaning technician check arch dcgm diag L [secs] dcgmi diag -r L reports no failure. Deep context only It follows part 6's rules, including one that testing this page added to the list: declare module globals with declare -g . More on that below. Install it next to the built-ins: /etc/nhc/scripts/acme arch.nhc . ---

secs.head: Step 4: prove it with real NHC before it ships
secs.body: Generated configs are only trustworthy if something executes them. NHC 1.5 can run straight from a Git clone and has three features that make a test harness easy: - NHC CFG CONFDIR / NHC CFG INCDIR point it at a test directory instead of /etc/nhc . - -m host masquerades as any node, so one CI runner can test every class. - Module command variables ( ARCH NVSMI , ARCH NUMA ONLINE ) and NHC DMESG CMD can point at fakes. [!WARNING] Run these tests only in CI or a throwaway container. MARK OFFLINE=0 stops draining, not fixing: checks with auto-fix flags still act. In testing, NHC tried to start sshd and munge and created /scratch and /apps on the test machine. nhc test harness.sh refuses to run outside CI or a container unless you pass --force . Test 1: does each node get the right lines? Count the checks selected per host: Real results for the example cluster: Host Checks Why ------ -------: ----- cn100 15 4 global + 11 for cpu-std cn500 15 4 global + 11 for cpu-bigmem (different memory size, same count) gpu07 25 4 global + 21 for gpu-h100 (8 HCA lines) gpu31 4 Out for RMA: excluded from the class, globals only ✅ login01 11 4 global + 7 for login (no scratch, no hygiene) storage01 4 Not in the architecture: globals only gpu07 epilog 8 Mounts and GPU lines only Turn that table into assertions and a change that accidentally drops a class's checks fails CI. Test 2: do the checks pass on a good node and fail on a bad one? Fake the hardware: Test 3: does the Xid line catch a fatal Xid? Prepend a line that swaps dmesg for a fake log: Real hardware failures are rare and you can't schedule them. Fakes let you prove every check fails when it should, on every commit. All three tests in one script. nhc test harness.sh runs them with assertions. Expected check counts per host live in a block at the top; update them when cluster.yaml changes. On the example cluster: With the backslash bug from the next section put back into the config, it reports FAIL - Xid check does NOT fail on fatal Xid 79 and exits 1. ---

secs.head: Two traps the tests caught
secs.body: Both of these were in the first draft of this series. Neither shows up when you test checks with nhc -e , only when real NHC reads a real config and loads a real module. That's the whole argument for Step 4. Trap 1: backslashes vanish from config lines. The Xid regex was first written with \(PCI:...\) . Through nhc -e it worked. Through the config file it passed even with Xid 79 in the log : NHC's config parser drops backslashes, \( became ( , and the regex turned into a group that can never match the real line. A health check that always passes is worse than none, because it looks like coverage. The fix is bracket expressions, which need no escaping: [(] , [)] , [[] , []] , [.] . The generator emits only those. Part 3 now carries a warning about it. Trap 2: module variables that disappear. check arch numa nodes first failed with cannot read and an empty path. NHC loads modules by sourcing them inside a function , and in bash a plain declare inside a function makes a local variable. The module's defaults existed only while the file was being loaded. It hid in testing because passing ARCH NVSMI=... on the command line sets a global that masks the bug, while on a real node, with no override, every GPU node would have drained with "nvidia-smi failed". Fix: declare -g . Part 6 now lists it as a rule. A third thing worth knowing from the harness: when NHC couldn't find its modules (a wrong INCDIR ), it still ended with "completed successfully; 0 passed" . Treat "0 passed" as a failure in your tests and your monitoring. ---

secs.head: Step 5: ship it through CI
secs.body: A minimal pipeline, here as GitHub Actions; the shape is the same in GitLab or Jenkins: Then deliver build/ and acme arch.nhc the way you deliver any config: an RPM such as acme-nhc-config (with Requires: lbnl-nhc , versioned per Git tag, which makes rollback a dnf downgrade ), or your Ansible role from part 2. The rollout itself is still dry run, canary, enforce, behind the circuit breaker (part 5). Generation makes the config correct ; it doesn't make it safe to push to 2,000 nodes at once . [!TIP] Keep slurm.conf and cluster.yaml in the same repository. Then a pull request that adds nodes to Slurm but not to the architecture fails its own CI, and the reviewer sees both halves of the change in one diff. ---

secs.head: Onboarding a new hardware generation
secs.body: The payoff. A new rack of 64 GPU nodes arrives with a different GPU model and a different NUMA layout: 1. Add one class to cluster.yaml : gpu-next , nodes: "gpx[01-64]" , its CPU, NUMA, memory, fabric and gpus block. 2. Add the NodeName line to slurm.conf in the same pull request. 3. CI generates and tests. Forgot the Slurm line? Forgot the class? Typo in the GPU count? The build fails and says which. 4. Bring the rack up in canary mode (part 5), then into production. Every new node gets health checks on day one, without anyone writing an NHC line. ---

secs.head: Growing the model
secs.body: The example covers the essentials. Common next additions, each a YAML field plus a few generator lines: Architecture fact How to check it ------------------- ----------------- BIOS version, SMT, power profile check dmi data match against dmidecode data Kernel and driver versions check file contents /proc/sys/kernel/osrelease '<version ' and /proc/driver/nvidia/version NVLink / GPU topology Golden copy of nvidia-smi topo -m per class, compared by a small module check HCA firmware and port GUIDs ibstat output through check cmd output CPU frequency governor, THP, hugepages check file contents on /sys files (part 6) Local NVMe scratch check fs mount rw plus check fs size per class One honest limit: everything here is still a per-node truth. A cluster where every node passes can still have a degraded fabric path or one slow GPU dragging a 512-GPU job (related reading). Multi-node tests (NCCL, MPI benchmarks) are the layer above, and they can be generated from the same architecture file. Takeaway: describe the cluster once, generate NHC from it, refuse to build when it disagrees with slurm.conf or leaves nodes uncovered, and run every generated config through real NHC with fakes in CI. The tests on this page found two silent bugs that hand-written configs and nhc -e testing never would have.

secs.head: References
secs.body: - NHC README: match strings, contexts, -m masquerade, NHC CFG overrides - NHC 1.5 release notes - slurm.conf : node configuration ( NodeName , RealMemory , Gres ) - NVIDIA Xid errors catalogue

label: 10. Case study: build us an NHC
title: Case Study: "Build Us an NHC", From a Vague Ask to a Validated Proposal
desc: Part 10 of the Node Health Check series. The final exam. Everything from parts 1-9, applied to one realistic engagement:

secs.head: Case Study: "Build Us an NHC", From a Vague Ask to a Validated Proposal
secs.body: Part 10 of the Node Health Check series. The final exam. Everything from parts 1-9, applied to one realistic engagement: a vague request, ten minutes of thinking, a discovery call, a first proposal, a coffee, a validation pass that changes the proposal, and the answer that goes back. [!NOTE] What's real here. The client and their names are invented. The hardware is not: every spec comes from NVIDIA's and AMD's published documentation (linked in References). Every command output on this page was produced by running the series' tools ( nhc gen.py , nhc test harness.sh ) against this cluster's definition with real NHC 1.5. The inputs are in case-study-delta-cluster.yaml and case-study-delta-expected.txt .

secs.head: The ask
secs.body: Tuesday, 09:12. An email from the head of research computing at a university we'll call Delta : "Hi, we keep losing GPU jobs. Researchers say training runs hang at startup on some nodes, mostly after maintenance, and every few weeks a batch of CPU jobs dies with I/O errors. A colleague told us we need 'NHC'. Can you build us an NHC for our cluster? We run Slurm. How fast can you do it?" It's tempting to reply with a link to part 3 and a sample config. Don't. "Build us an NHC" is a solution the client picked. Our job is to find the problem first. ---

secs.head: The ten minutes before you reply
secs.body: Before typing a word, think through what you know and what you don't. Here's what those ten minutes look like on paper. 1. Read the symptoms like a detective. Symptom from the email Plausible causes What would detect it --- --- --- GPU jobs "hang at startup" on some nodes NVSwitch fabric not initialized (a known cause of CUDA error 802 on DGX/HGX), a GPU missing, an IB rail down so NCCL stalls GPU count, fabric state, per-HCA link checks "Mostly after maintenance" Services not started after reboot, nodes returning to the pool before they're ready Boot-time checks; NHC keeping rebooted nodes drained until checks pass (part 4) CPU jobs die with I/O errors, in batches Lustre client evictions or a dropped mount on a subset of nodes: the classic black hole (part 1) Mount checks with type and source "Some nodes" Heterogeneous hardware, or drift between identical nodes Per-class expectations (part 9) 2. List what you don't know but must. Hardware classes and counts. Slurm version and current health-check settings. Who drains nodes today, and how. What tools already exist (NVSM, DCGM, monitoring). Operating systems. How they deploy config. How much automatic draining they'll tolerate. Who gets paged. 3. Name the risks of getting it wrong. A bad config drains the whole cluster (part 5). Two tools both draining nodes fight each other. Expensive checks on GPU nodes slow training. Auto-fixes that hide hardware faults void the evidence the vendor will ask for. 4. Decide what to send back now. Not a solution: a short reply that shows you understood, sets expectations, and asks for a discovery call plus a small data bundle. The reply, sent at 09:25: "Thanks. What you're describing (hangs after maintenance, batches of I/O failures) is exactly what node health checking is good at, so NHC is a reasonable direction. Before proposing anything, I'd like a 45-minute call and a few command outputs from one node of each type (list attached). That lets me propose checks that match your hardware instead of a generic template. Expect a written proposal within two working days of the call." ---

secs.head: Discovery: the questions, and why each one matters
secs.body: A question you can't connect to a decision is a question you shouldn't ask. Each one below states the decision it drives. Problem and expectations Question Why it matters --- --- What fails, how often, and since when? Any ticket numbers or job IDs? Gives a baseline, so we can later prove the fix worked What does "done" look like for you? Becomes the acceptance criteria How many false drains per week would be acceptable? Sets how strict thresholds can be Scheduler and node state Question Why it matters --- --- Slurm version? Current HealthCheck settings? Which HealthCheckNodeState values exist; whether anything runs today Who drains nodes today, and do they always set a reason? The NHC: ownership contract (part 1) only works if humans use reasons Do you reboot nodes with scontrol reboot ? ASAP ? Decides whether NHC 1.5's reboot handling matters, and how remediation must call it (part 7) Existing Prolog/Epilog scripts? Job-boundary checks must fit around them Hardware and OS Question Why it matters --- --- Every node type: model, CPUs, RAM, GPUs, HCAs, local disks One class per distinct build BIOS settings that matter: SMT, NUMA per socket (NPS) Thread and NUMA checks must expect the configured values, not the maximum OS and version per node type Packaging (RPM vs source), sysconfig path, helper paths Any nodes out for repair right now? Exclude them from classes instead of drowning the first rollout in known failures Fabric and storage Question Why it matters --- --- Which HCAs carry compute traffic vs storage, and at what rate? IB checks per compute HCA; don't IB-check Ethernet ports Shared filesystems: mount points, types, servers Mount checks with type and source; avoid df on network mounts Local scratch on nodes? Its own mount check GPUs Question Why it matters --- --- NVSwitch systems (DGX/HGX)? How is Fabric Manager run? Fabric checks become mandatory Driver and DCGM versions Check commands and output formats Which Xid errors have you seen? Calibrates the drain list against real history Existing tooling and operations Question Why it matters --- --- What else monitors or acts on node health (NVSM, BCM, DCGM exporter, custom scripts)? Avoids two tools fighting over node state How is config deployed (Ansible, xCAT, image)? Is it in Git? Delivery path and rollback Is there a test node or partition we can use? Canary rollout (part 5) Who acts on a drained node, and how fast? Decides how much auto-remediation is worth building Change windows, approvals? Timeline The data bundle we asked for (one node of each type, run as root): ---

That node was the hang : CUDA can't initialize until the NVSwitch fabric is formed, even though the Fabric Manager process is up. NVIDIA's troubleshooting docs list fabric state as the thing to check for CUDA error 802 on NVSwitch systems. 2. Five nodes drained with empty reasons . Nobody remembered why. NHC will leave those alone, and someone needs to triage them before rollout. ---

secs.head: The first proposal
secs.body: Drafted right after the call (call it version 0.1): - NHC 1.5 on all nodes, run by slurmd every 300 s, HealthCheckNodeState=ANY,CYCLE . - Configs generated from one architecture definition (part 9), with three contexts: periodic, epilog, deep. - Per class: mounts, CPU/NUMA/memory, IB per HCA, services, rogue-process logging; on DGX also GPU count, GPU model, Xid scan, DCGM level 2 in the deep context only. - Rollout: dry run, canary on 2 DGX + 8 CPU nodes, enforce behind a circuit breaker (part 5). - Remediation (phase 2): node doctor reboots for a short list of failures, max 2 per day per node (part 7). It looks complete. It isn't. ---

secs.head: ☕ Coffee, then validation
secs.body: Coffee isn't a joke step. Stepping away is how you stop reviewing your own draft as its author. Back at the desk, the rule is: every claim in the proposal gets checked against a primary source or a test run. Here's what that pass found. Draft assumption What validation showed Change --- --- --- --- 1 DGX compute HCAs are mlx5 0 … mlx5 7 NVIDIA's port table: compute ports are mlx5 0,3,4,5,6,9,10,11 ; 1,2,7,8 are the storage cards, Ethernet by default IB checks on the 8 real compute HCAs only. A naive config would fail on every DGX, every run 2 "Fabric Manager running" = GPUs usable The client's own data showed FM active with fabric In Progress . Process liveness isn't fabric health New check check arch gpu fabric : every GPU must report Completed, Success . FM service check kept, with -S to restart it 3 Drain on Xid 48, 79, 94, 95, 119 NVIDIA's GPU debug guidelines: 94 (contained ECC) needs only the affected application restarted; 92 is informational; 64 and 95 need a reboot. Google Cloud's GPU troubleshooting guide: stop workloads and reset GPUs on 74 (NVLink) and 119 (GSP timeout) Drain list becomes 48, 64, 74, 79, 95, 119, 120. Xid 94 goes to monitoring, not drains. (The client's Xid 13/31 history is application-side and correctly ignored) 4 slurm.conf matches hardware The generator's cross-check failed on the first run (output below): slurm.conf says 1 thread per core on EPYC nodes; the hardware has SMT on Question for the client: intended or not? Must be resolved before rollout 5 One package for everyone DGX OS is Ubuntu-based; CPU nodes are Rocky 9 RPM for Rocky; build from the release tarball for DGX OS, with /etc/default/nhc as its sysconfig path (part 2) 6 DCGM level 2 in the deep context is fine anywhere Level 2 runs about two minutes and loads the GPUs; Slurm kills the health check at 60 s Confirmed: deep context only, never periodic, with its own TIMEOUT=900 7 NHC is the only health tool DGX OS ships NVSM, which does its own health monitoring and alerting Ownership rule: NVSM and DCGM alert , only NHC drains . Written into the runbook 8 Login nodes are like compute nodes They're not Slurm nodes, so the cross-check would flag them as missing from slurm.conf Marked in slurm: false ; no hygiene checks on login nodes 9 /raid is ext4 on /dev/md That's what the client's findmnt showed on dgx01 Kept, but verified on all 16 DGX during the dry run before enforcing Findings 2 and 8 needed new capabilities in the series' tools: a service map and extra services in the YAML for Fabric Manager, the check arch gpu fabric module check, in slurm: false , and a harness that accepts a client's expectations. They're now part of nhc gen.py , acme arch.nhc and nhc test harness.sh . Finding 4, as the generator reported it. The node lines from the client's slurm.conf : The cross-check: The client checked lscpu on cpu001 : 2 threads per core. They chose to fix slurm.conf ( ThreadsPerCore=2 , saved as client-slurm-fixed.conf ) and use --hint=nomultithread where jobs need full cores. After that: The generated DGX block (periodic context, target {dgx[01-16]} omitted): The test run , real NHC 1.5 with fake GPUs and kernel logs (part 9): The fabric test reproduces the client's hang: with every GPU at In Progress, N/A , NHC reports check arch gpu fabric: GPU 0 fabric is 'In Progress, N/A' (Fabric Manager not ready or fabric degraded) , which in production becomes the node's NHC: drain reason. That's the symptom from the original email, caught before a job lands. ---

secs.head: The answer back to the client
secs.body: Thursday, 16:40, two working days after the call as promised. The proposal, as sent: Delta Research Computing: Node Health Check proposal (v1.0) Summary. Your GPU job hangs match a known NVSwitch failure mode: on at least one DGX, the GPU fabric wasn't initialized although Fabric Manager was running, and CUDA can't start in that state. Your batches of CPU I/O failures match nodes that keep accepting jobs after losing a filesystem. We propose LBNL NHC 1.5, configured from a single description of your cluster, to take such nodes out of service automatically with a readable reason, and to return them once healthy. What gets checked Node type Every 5 minutes (staggered) After every job On demand / after repairs --- --- --- --- DGX H100 ×16 Mounts ( /home , /lustre/scratch , /raid ), 8 GPUs present, NVSwitch fabric ready, fatal GPU errors, Fabric Manager/munge/sshd running (auto-restart), CPU, NUMA, memory, 8 × NDR links at 400 Gb/s, GPU model Mounts, GPUs, fabric, fatal GPU errors Everything, plus DCGM diagnostics level 2 EPYC ×120 Mounts, services, CPU (SMT on), NUMA (NPS1), memory, HDR link Mounts Everything Login ×2 Mounts, services, CPU, memory, HDR link (alerts only) — — What changes in Slurm. Three slurm.conf lines ( HealthCheckProgram , HealthCheckInterval=300 , HealthCheckNodeState=ANY,CYCLE ), a short epilog, and ThreadsPerCore=2 for the EPYC nodes (already agreed). How we roll it out (no node is drained by NHC until week 3) Week Step Exit criterion --- --- --- 1 Install, dry run on all nodes, triage every finding with you Every failure explained: config fixed or node fixed 2 Canary: NHC may drain only dgx[01-02] and cpu[001-008] 5 working days, zero false drains 3 Enforce everywhere, with an alert if more than 5% of nodes are NHC-drained You sign off 4-5 Optional phase 2: automatic reboot for a short list of GPU and service failures, max 2 per node per day, then escalation to you Agreed list, dry-run log reviewed How you'll know it worked. Baseline from your last 60 days: GPU jobs failing in the first 5 minutes, CPU jobs failing on I/O, hours that drained nodes sit unexplained. We report the same numbers 30 days after week 3. New rules for your team (one-page runbook included): always drain with a reason; reasons starting with NHC: belong to NHC; NVSM and DCGM alert, only NHC drains; change node expectations only through the cluster description in Git, which is tested automatically before deployment. What we need from you. Root access to one node per type and to the Slurm controller; a 30-minute slot to apply slurm.conf changes; a decision on the 5 nodes currently drained without a reason. Deliverables. Cluster description, generated configs, check module, test harness and CI pipeline, all in your Git repository; packages for Rocky 9 and DGX OS; runbook; a handover session. Out of scope. Multi-node performance validation (NCCL/MPI benchmarks across nodes), which we recommend as a follow-up: a node can pass every check and still slow a 16-node job. Open questions. (1) Confirm /raid is ext4 on all 16 DGX (verified on dgx01 only). (2) Who should be emailed for escalations in phase 2? Notice what the answer does not contain: NHC syntax, bash, or the word "match string". The client asked for an outcome. The technical depth lives in the deliverables and the runbook. ---

secs.head: The reusable checklist
secs.body: For the next "build us an NHC" email: 1. Before replying: map each symptom to plausible causes and to what would detect it. Reply with understanding, a discovery call and a data bundle, not a config. 2. Discovery: problem and success criteria; scheduler version, drain habits, reboot habits; every hardware class, with BIOS settings; OS per class; compute vs storage HCAs; mounts; GPU platform (NVSwitch?), driver, Xid history; other health tools; deployment method; test nodes; who acts on drains. 3. Ask for data, not descriptions: sinfo -R , slurm.conf node lines, lscpu , ibdev2netdev , findmnt , nvidia-smi fabric state, dmesg Xids. Clients describe the cluster they designed; commands show the cluster they have. 4. First proposal: classes and contexts, Slurm settings, rollout phases, remediation as a separate phase. 5. Validate every assumption against vendor documentation and a real test run: device names, service names, what "healthy" looks like, error policies, timeouts, OS differences, overlapping tools. Expect the proposal to change. Ours changed in 9 places. 6. Answer in the client's language: what was wrong, what gets checked, what changes, how it rolls out, how success is measured, what you need from them, what's out of scope. Takeaway: "build us an NHC" is the client's chosen solution, not their problem. Ten minutes of thinking turns it into the right questions; data beats descriptions; and a coffee-separated validation pass, against vendor docs and real test runs, is what turns a plausible proposal into one that works on their hardware. ---

secs.body: Path Purpose ------ --------- /usr/sbin/nhc , nhc-genconf , nhc-wrapper Programs /etc/nhc/<context .conf Config per context /etc/nhc/scripts/ .nhc Check modules ( .nhc required) /etc/sysconfig/<context or /etc/default/<context Early settings /usr/libexec/nhc/node-mark-{offline,online} RM helpers /var/log/nhc.log Run log /var/run/nhc/ Detached results, PID file (1.5)

secs.head: The rules, in eight lines
secs.body: 1. A fast-failing node is a black hole; NHC is the bouncer. 2. NHC: -prefixed reasons are NHC's; everything else is a human's. 3. Cheap checks, often. Expensive checks, rarely and elsewhere. 4. NHC's timeout below Slurm's. 5. Dry run, canary, enforce, behind a circuit breaker. 6. Every custom check: namespaced, cached, timed out, proven to fail. 7. Automate cheap fixes; budget retries; escalate by dropping the NHC: prefix. 8. Read the reason, rerun with -a -v -l- MARK OFFLINE=0 .
